Reasoning surface

The Binary Totient Series

Erdős #249

Native MathML copy. For the TeX-rendered copy with linked references, read the exact-TeX version.

Reading guide

The short paper gives a direct proof of the basis theorem and its integral normal form. This longer record is organised for reference. The opening section introduces the finite residue test and its quantified form, Definition 1.2. Section 2 gives rational comparison sequences, and Section 3 states four possible arithmetic conditions for irrationality. The detailed formulas then begin with the series identities and denominator bound in Section 5.3. The basis and relation modules are revisited in Section 10.8.

Two distinctions recur. “Cofinal” means that a condition holds at some index beyond each threshold; it does not mean that it holds at every sufficiently large index. A counterexample excludes only the hypotheses it satisfies. Agreement with a finite totient prefix, for example, need not preserve multiplicativity.

The annotations identify the kind of support: [Lean] refers to a formal statement and its pinned source or supplied checking record; [Cert] to a finite computation; [Math] to an ordinary argument; [Cited] to a literature result; and [Open] to an unproved assertion. The Lean kernel was not rerun for this revision. In particular, a checked implication does not establish its hypothesis.

Totient sections and tail differences

Let φ\varphi be Euler’s totient function, with φ(0)=0\varphi(0)=0, and use ℕ={0,1,2,…}\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}. The dyadic sections n↦φ(2jn+r)n\mapsto\varphi(2^jn+r), for 0≤j≤e0\le j\le e and 0≤r<2j0\le r<2^j, have rational rank 2e+12^e+1 when e≥1e\ge1. A basis consists of n↦φ(n)n\mapsto\varphi(n), n↦φ(2n)n\mapsto\varphi(2n), and the sections with odd rr at levels 1≤j≤e1\le j\le e. For example, φ(4n)=2φ(2n)\varphi(4n)=2\varphi(2n) and φ(4n+2)=φ(2n+1)\varphi(4n+2)=\varphi(2n+1) recover the omitted sections at level two. The short paper proves the corresponding rank ke+1k^e+1 in every integer base k≥2k\ge2, together with the integral coordinates and relations. For composite kk, the retained condition is k∤rk\nmid r, not gcd⁡(k,r)=1\gcd(k,r)=1.

The question about the series concerns more than these coefficient relations. Put S:=∑n≥1φ(n)2n=12+14+28+216+432+⋯=1.3676308019850223…S \;:=\; \sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{\varphi(n)}{2^{n}} \;=\; \tfrac12 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac{2}{8} + \tfrac{2}{16} + \tfrac{4}{32} + \cdots \;=\; 1.3676308019850223\ldots The series converges absolutely because φ(n)≤n\varphi(n) \le n. Erdős Problem #249 asks whether SS is irrational, which remains open. The exact rank theorem controls linear relations among coefficient sections. Irrationality requires information about their weighted infinite sum. The countermodels below explain several ways that a passage from coefficient structure to the sum can fail. Each excludes its stated assumptions; they do not establish a single obstruction theorem covering all possible methods.

Remark 1.1 (Earlier coefficient results). Erdős and Graham record the irrationality question for SS . An integer sequence is kk-regular when the ℤ\mathbb{Z}-module generated by its sections n↦c(kjn+r)n\mapsto c(k^jn+r), j≥0j\ge0 and 0≤r<kj0\le r<k^j, is finitely generated. Coons proved that φ\varphi is not kk-regular for any k≥2k\ge2 . Martin’s Theorem 1 implies that the functions n↦φ(ain+bi)n\mapsto\varphi(a_in+b_i) are linearly independent for pairwise nonproportional affine forms with positive integer slopes [4]. The exact ranks in §10.8, together with the all-base normal form in the short paper, identify the retained sections and every relation among them. The independence itself is not claimed as new. The CRT–Dirichlet separation method is already present in Yazdani’s Theorem 2 and proof, which explicitly credit Shallit [28]; our evaluation matrix uses one such separation for each column. Yazdani also proves non-automaticity of φ(n)mod⁡m\varphi(n)\operatorname{mod} m for every m≥3m\ge3 in every base [28]. Allouche, Shallit and Yassawi give a survey account .

Thus it suffices, for every positive shift hh, to find arbitrarily large NN for which RN+h−RNR_{N+h}-R_N is not an integer. A finite test is obtained by truncating this difference. The error bound N+h+L+2N{+}h{+}L{+}2 comes from φ(m)≤m\varphi(m) \le m, so a certificate is sound: it forces RN+h−RN∉ℤR_{N+h} - R_N \notin \mathbb{Z}, and in fact certificates are complete for non-integrality (). The resulting quantified condition is the following.

Definition 1.2 (The quantified residue condition). Sep:⇔∀h≥1∀N0∃N≥N0∃L,𝒞(h,N,L).\mathrm{Sep} \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; \forall h \ge 1\ \forall N_0\ \exists N \ge N_0\ \exists L,\; \mathcal{C}(h,N,L). Sep⇔S∉ℚ\mathrm{Sep} \Longleftrightarrow S\notin\mathbb Q (). The forward implication is also . The equivalence identifies the missing quantified input; it supplies no certificate by itself. [cofinal] [Lean]

The order of the quantifiers matters. A certificate at one (h,N,L)(h,N,L) excludes those hypothetical rational values whose denominator divides 2N(2h−1)2^N(2^h-1); it does not exclude all denominators. The condition above asks for certificates beyond every threshold for each positive hh, and is therefore exactly as strong as the original irrationality assertion. Its depth must grow: the two strict residue inequalities imply 2(N+h+L+2)<2L2(N+h+L+2)<2^L. Keeping LL fixed cannot provide certificates as NN grows. Neither this necessary size condition nor a finite list of successful tests supplies the required residues.

Unconditional results

The following results require no irrationality hypothesis. The finite denominator bound concerns rational values of SS; the rank and positivity results concern its coefficients and tails. The latter do not by themselves exclude rationality.

Theorem 1.3 (Denominator exclusion from a fixed Farey window). If S∈ℚS \in \mathbb{Q} then its reduced denominator exceeds Q0:=79639646646701375323355774875831053≈7.96×1034Q_0 := 79\,639\,646\,646\,701\,375\,323\,355\,774\,875\,831\,053 \approx 7.96 \times 10^{34}. Equivalently, SS differs from every rational number whose reduced denominator is at most Q0Q_0. The bound is sharp for this window: q=Q0+1q = Q_0 + 1 is the exact first failing denominator. It is the denominator of the mediant of two explicit unimodular Farey neighbours. [bounded] [Lean]

To deduce irrationality by this argument, the analogous denominator bounds would have to be unbounded as the window grows; this has not been proved. [Open]

For the next two propositions, a rational value S=a/vS=a/v, with integers aa and v≥1v\ge1, would give the integer carry uN=vRN=2Na−vΦN,uN+1=2uN−vφ(N+1),0≤uN≤v(N+2).u_N=vR_N=2^Na-v\Phi_N,\qquad u_{N+1}=2u_N-v\varphi(N+1),\qquad 0\le u_N\le v(N+2). Proposition 1.6 (Rationality forces unbounded carry rank). If SS is rational then, for every ee, the carry sections n↦u2jn+rn\mapsto u_{2^jn+r} with 1≤j≤e1\le j\le e and 0≤r<2j0\le r<2^j span a rational vector space of dimension at least 2e−12^{e}-1 (). The lower bound holds at every depth. It comes from the linear independence of the 2e+12^e+1 retained dyadic totient sections for e≥1e\ge1, proved using the Chinese remainder theorem and Dirichlet’s theorem (), so the full family spans an infinite-dimensional space (), the case k=2k=2 of Coons’s non-regularity theorem (§10.8). [uniform] [Lean]

Proposition 1.7 (Periodicity modulo an integer does not bound rational rank). If SS is rational, the same carry uu has unbounded rational section rank and one eventual period modulo vv valid for all its dyadic sections. More precisely, there are h≥1h\ge1 and N0N_0 such that, for every j,r≥0j,r\ge0 and n≥N0n\ge N_0, u2j(n+h)+r≡u2jn+r(mod⁡v).u_{2^j(n+h)+r}\equiv u_{2^jn+r}\pmod v. The rank and periodicity assertions hold together (). This conditional theorem alone is not a counterexample to a general periodicity-to-rank implication: its antecedent is not established. The separate 5/45/4 control supplies a concrete counterexample to the generic rationality-driven rank ceiling; see the detailed comparison in Section 10.8. [uniform] [Lean]

These propositions separate several logical obligations. Positivity leaves an upper-endpoint condition; a large rational carry rank is not a contradiction; and exact equivalences still require a quantified certificate condition. The stated size bounds, parity and aperiodicity also hold for a rational control. Each conclusion concerns its stated hypotheses, not all possible arithmetic information about φ\varphi.

Rational comparison sequences

The countermodels distinguish information that determines a finite calculation from information that forces nonintegrality at unbounded indices. A fixed prefix, parity at every index, and a specified finite collection of linear relations are different hypotheses. The useful conclusion in each case is the precise information a rational control sequence can preserve.

What finite information does not determine

The comparison sequences below preserve different parts of the totient data. Theorem 2.4 preserves an arbitrary fixed prefix. Proposition 1.9 preserves parity at every index, together with size bounds and aperiodicity. Propositions 2.13 and 2.14 address particular carry descriptions and linear constructions, not every finite-state or finite-dimensional argument.

Two other limitations do not require a rational comparison sequence. A congruence construction can increase the index so much that its tail error exceeds the residue it produces (Proposition 2.11). An exact reformulation or a finite list of examples still needs the quantified arithmetic assertion (Proposition 2.7 and Remark 2.9).

The finite certificates in Proposition 1.4 and the K=240K=240 Farey calculation in Theorem 1.3 have bounded ranges. Theorem 2.4 excludes an inference from one such fixed range uniformly over the whole coefficient class. It does not exclude a proof using the arithmetic of φ\varphi at arbitrarily large horizons. Likewise, the cofinal positivity theorem does not by itself separate the residue from the top edge: that is the additional information identified by Proposition 1.5.

A rational sequence with any prescribed totient prefix

A finite prefix leaves the remaining coefficients free. We construct a rational continuation satisfying the same linear size bound, then show why it cannot satisfy the quantified residue condition. First we record the two tail facts needed for a general coefficient sequence. For c:ℕ→ℕc : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} with c(n)≤nc(n) \le n, write Tc:=∑n≥1c(n)/2nT_c := \sum_{n \ge 1} c(n)/2^{n}, RNc:=∑j≥0c(N+1+j)/2j+1R^{c}_{N} := \sum_{j \ge 0} c(N{+}1{+}j)/2^{\,j+1}, Dc(h,N,L):=∑j<L(c(N+h+1+j)−c(N+1+j))2L−1−jD_c(h,N,L) := \sum_{j<L}(c(N{+}h{+}1{+}j) - c(N{+}1{+}j))2^{\,L-1-j}, and let 𝒞c(h,N,L)\mathcal C_c(h,N,L) and Sepc\mathrm{Sep}_c be 𝒞\mathcal{C} and Sep\mathrm{Sep} with DcD_c in place of D{D}. Corollary 2.5 (The limit of a finite-prefix argument). No proof rule uniform over all c:ℕ→ℕc:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} with c(n)≤nc(n)\le n can establish Sep\mathrm{Sep} from a single fixed prefix {c(n):n≤B}\{c(n):n\le B\}: Theorem 2.4 supplies a rational countermodel with that same prefix. This does not invalidate an argument that uses the fixed arithmetic sequence φ\varphi together with compatible information at arbitrarily large horizons; the theorem gives a different γB\gamma_B for each BB, not one sequence agreeing with φ\varphi at every BB.

Remark 2.6 (Four distinct finite restrictions). Theorem 2.4 concerns the information in a finite prefix. It does not identify φ\varphi with one of the comparison sequences. It also does not exclude a proof that combines finite computation with an arithmetic theorem applying at all larger indices. Four different restrictions must be kept separate: a bound on the indices inspected, a bound on the depth LL, a bound on the carry states retained, and a bound on matrix rank. The depth inequality 2(N+h+L+2)<2L2(N+h+L+2)<2^L, for example, concerns the second restriction, not all four.

Proposition 1.9 gives another rational comparison sequence, this time preserving parity and specified aperiodicity properties. The two examples test different assumptions and must not be combined into a single stronger example.

Limits of specific reductions and estimates

The following results concern specified assumptions, not all possible proof methods. Statements labelled as an audit describe the finite set of arguments examined in that audit. They are not mathematical impossibility theorems.

Proposition 2.7 (Three particular equivalences).

  1. Certificate completeness. The complete residue tests considered here are equivalent to the corresponding nonintegrality assertions. Rewriting the quantified condition using one of these equivalences does not weaken it (, forward at :132, converse at :143).

  2. A selectable two-point sample. The condition is as follows. Remark 2.8. Second-difference certificates need not occur at a smaller depth than first-difference certificates. At (h,N)=(1,8)(h,N)=(1,8), the first-difference test holds at depth 88, whereas no second-difference certificate exists at a depth at most 88 (certificate kernel source:18762, [Lean]). This one example refutes a uniform claim that second differences always save depth; it does not give a uniform ordering in the opposite direction.

Separately, unbounded growth of the denominator exclusions produced by the Farey windows would imply irrationality. The record does not establish a converse for that specific sequence of windows, so the proposed growth condition is used only as a sufficient condition. [Math]

Remark 2.9 (A finite audit of proposed extensions). This is a report of a finite audit. The audit listed 5656 candidate deductions for four stated goals and examined 1818 proposed extensions. Its recorded verdict was 1616 not accepted as routine extensions and 22 accepted only as restatements for a wider target family. One of the 1616, labelled NM-12 in the audit, was not verified because the endpoint proofs were not read. Thus it is not correct to say that all 1818 proof bodies were checked or that all 1616 negative verdicts were proved. The recorded categories were hypothesis strength (66), parameter range (55), representation (44), and multiple issues (33). Neither accepted extension supplied the arithmetic assertion needed for irrationality. No conclusion about arguments outside this finite audit follows. [n/a] [Cert]

Several unsuccessful arguments in the audit sought one certificate at a specially chosen large index, whereas the exponential-sum criterion seeks cancellation across an entire block. This is a difference in the statements being attempted, not evidence that one approach is the only possible one. The older list ending at t=64t=64 is not the current finite record: the supplied sources certify every diagonal scale 1≤t≤821\le t\le82. Neither list proves the required assertion for arbitrarily large scales.

What the counterexamples establish

The counterexamples isolate several distinctions. Finite prefix data are not a statement about all larger indices. A congruence construction can produce a large residue while producing an even larger error bound. Periodicity modulo an integer does not control rational rank. An exact reformulation leaves the original arithmetic assertion to be proved.

These are limitations of specified arguments, not an exhaustive classification of possible methods. In particular, an averaging estimate is one possible source of the missing information, not the only possible source. A new arithmetic identity or a propagation theorem could also be useful. The next section describes the precise assumptions of several approaches considered here.

Conditions that would imply irrationality

Four conditions considered below would imply irrationality. The first three ask for quantitative estimates; the fourth is an exact reformulation of irrationality. We also record a generic rank assertion that is false, to prevent its being mistaken for an open sufficient hypothesis. None of this is an exhaustive list of approaches. For each condition the question is whether its particular arithmetic hypothesis can be proved.

Cancellation on a full block

Definition 3.1 (The full-block norm condition). Write e(x):=exp⁡(2πix)e(x) := \exp(2\pi i x) and E(h,N,L):=e((D(h,N,L)mod⁡2L)/2L){E}(h,N,L) := e\bigl(({D}(h,N,L) \operatorname{mod} 2^{L})/2^{L}\bigr). The block norm condition asserts that ∀h≥1∀X0∃X,L:max⁡(X0,1)≤X,16(2X+h+L+2)≤2L,∥∑N∈[X,2X)E(h,N,L)∥≤2125X.\forall h \ge 1\ \forall X_0\ \exists X, L : \quad \max(X_0,1) \le X, \quad 16(2X + h + L + 2) \le 2^{L}, \quad \Bigl\lVert \sum_{N \in [X,\,2X)} {E}(h,N,L) \Bigr\rVert \le \tfrac{21}{25}X . It implies S∉ℚS\notin\mathbb Q. [cofinal] [Lean]

A bound on the real part also suffices: it is enough that ∑N∈[X,2X)Re⁡E(h,N,L)≤910X\sum_{N \in [X,2X)} \operatorname{Re}E(h,N,L) \le \tfrac{9}{10}X (, the elementary real-part estimate; the implication from 21/2521/25 to 9/109/10 is ). Unpacked, the required object is a constant-saving cancellation estimate for the dyadically weighted totient-difference exponential sum ∑X≤N<2Xe(∑j<L(φ(N+h+1+j)−φ(N+1+j))2L−1−j2L),L subject to the displayed room inequality.\sum_{X \le N < 2X} e\!\left(\frac{\sum_{j<L}\bigl(\varphi(N{+}h{+}1{+}j)-\varphi(N{+}1{+}j)\bigr)2^{\,L-1-j}}{2^{L}}\right), \qquad L \text{ subject to the displayed room inequality}. No theorem in the supplied record establishes this estimate with the required quantifiers. The displayed room inequality imposes a lower bound on LL; it does not require L=log⁡2X+O(1)L=\log_2X+O(1). A depth of that order would be a possible regime for the estimate, not an additional proved conclusion. A finite instance would not suffice. The norm hypothesis requires cancellation: if all phases are 11, the norm is XX and the bound fails; a balanced set of opposite phases has sum zero. If instead every phase is −1-1, the real part is −X-X and satisfies the real-part bound, while the norm is XX and fails the norm bound. Thus a real-part estimate is strictly weaker for general phase families; these examples do not distinguish the two quantified conditions for the actual totient sequence. The same depth LL must work across the whole block. [Open]

Comparison with the preceding counterexamples.

The earlier counterexamples do not establish or refute this block estimate. The following distinctions explain why those particular arguments do not settle it.

  • The parameters grow. The room condition forces the truncation depth to increase with XX, so this is not a test of a fixed prefix.

  • The sample is prescribed: all N∈[X,2X)N\in[X,2X) are summed at one depth. Choosing two favourable indices does not establish this block estimate.

  • The sum uses the accumulated totient differences. It does not prescribe individual values through a congruence construction.

  • The estimate concerns the actual phases. Neither a bound on carry rank nor agreement only in parity gives it.

  • The proved implication uses the real-part threshold 9/109/10 and the room constant 1616. The stronger norm bound 21/2521/25 implies that real-part bound. These constants do not assert any distribution theorem for the totient phases.

Remark 3.2 (The finite-prefix example does not choose a method). The finite-prefix example does not select an analytic method. It shows only that a proof valid for every sequence 0≤c(n)≤n0\le c(n)\le n cannot deduce the required assertion from one fixed prefix. An argument using additional identities of φ\varphi, a theorem propagating a finite base case, a Farey estimate, or a suitable exponential sum could provide information not contained in that prefix. The earlier finite audit cannot rank all such possibilities.

Remark 3.3 (Finite certificate observations). In the historical table of 2828 diagonal certificates through t=64t=64, the reported depths exceed the necessary depth bound by a small additive constant. A separate enumeration at the indices where the least common multiple increases records a closest margin from the central interval’s boundary of approximately 0.0002210.000221 of the modulus, at t=100t=100. Both are finite observations. Neither establishes nor refutes equidistribution or the estimate at arbitrarily large scales. [Cert]

Like the block criterion, this condition concerns actual totient values at arbitrarily large indices and at a common truncation depth. The four bounds are a sufficient way to prove the needed real-part estimate, not an equivalent restatement of the norm estimate.

The decomposition is an exact identity. The supplied formal record contains its unconditional proof and an axiom report (, budget implication ). The mean being subtracted is the mean of zNz_N, not of the residual weight wNw_N. This special choice has s=L−hs=L-h varying with LL; it illustrates the arithmetic of the groups but does not establish the condition with ss fixed before X0X_0.

The four inequalities are not proved with their required common parameters. Propositions 12.7 and 12.8 below do establish the unassigned and excluded-cofactor bounds at minimal admissible depth, with one sufficiently small fixed η\eta. The mean and mean-subtracted estimates remain to be established at that same depth and for that same η\eta. Only the real part of the mean-subtracted contribution is required.

A nonzero determinant alone does not prove the needed correlation estimate. The comparison in the linked source preserves such a determinant while fixing an entire row of weighted phases to 11. A successful application must distinguish that comparison, for example by additional arithmetic information, rather than only by column rescaling. The exact four-term identity supplies no prime-distribution estimate. [Open]

A fixed separation at prime positions

Definition 3.5 (A fixed gap at prime positions). For every h≥1h \ge 1 and every N0N_0 there is a prime pp with max⁡(N0+h+1,h+5)≤p\max(N_0{+}h{+}1,\, h{+}5) \le p and Ree(Rp−1−Rp−h−1)<910\mathrm{Re}\,e(R_{p-1}-R_{p-h-1}) < \tfrac{9}{10}, where e(x)=exp⁡(2πix)e(x)=\exp(2\pi i x). Equivalently: cofinally many primes pp at which the totient tail difference across the shift hh stays a fixed distance >arccos⁡(9/10)/(2π)≈0.0718> \arccos(9/10)/(2\pi) \approx 0.0718 from every integer. It implies S∉ℚS\notin\mathbb Q. [cofinal] [Lean]

This asks for more than nonintegrality. A nonintegral real number can be arbitrarily close to an integer, whereas the displayed condition requires a fixed positive distance, along prime positions and for each shift hh. For example, phases at a half-integer satisfy the numerical gap and phases converging to an integer eventually fail it. These are illustrations of the hypothesis, not assertions about the totient tails. No estimate for these tail differences at prime positions with the stated quantifiers is proved here. Certificate completeness alone does not supply it. [Open]

Certificates with depth equal to the shift

Definition 3.6 (Depth equal to a shift multiple). For every d≥1d \ge 1 and every NN there is t≥1t \ge 1 with 𝒞(td,N,td)\mathcal{C}(td,\,N,\,td); unpacked, N+2td+2<D(td,N,td)mod⁡2td<2td−(N+2td+2).N + 2td + 2 \;<\; {D}(td,N,td) \operatorname{mod} 2^{td} \;<\; 2^{td} - (N + 2td + 2). It is equivalent to S∉ℚS\notin\mathbb Q. [cofinal] [Lean]

For the actual totient series, the condition in Definition 3.6 is equivalent to irrationality, by the full-depth amplification argument of the short note (Theorem 3.1 there; ). For a fixed pair (d,N)(d,N), a nonintegral tail difference supplies a certificate in every sufficiently late adjacent pair of multipliers. The missing arithmetic input is a nonintegral tail difference for every relevant pair, not a converse implication for the condition with depth equal to the shift. This remains an exact reformulation of the open problem, not a proof of it. An older one-direction lemma () is still in the cited source; it is not the current classification.

The finite examples establish the hypothesis for individual pairs (d,N)(d,N), not for all pairs. Thus the universally quantified condition is not a mild regularity assumption: it has the full strength of the irrationality question. [Open]

A false generic rank bound

Definition 3.7 (A counterfactual rank criterion). The proposed assertion is a constant CC bounding the rank for every c:ℕ→ℕc:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} with c(n)≤nc(n)\le n and Tc∈ℚT_c\in\mathbb{Q}, every integer v>0v>0, and every integer sequence uu satisfying u(n+1)=2u(n)−vc(n+1),u(n)/2n→0.u(n+1)=2u(n)-v c(n+1),\qquad u(n)/2^n\longrightarrow0. Specifically, the proposed bound is dim⁡ℚspan⁡ℚ{n↦u(2jn+r):1≤j≤e,0≤r<2j}≤C(e≥0).\dim_{\mathbb{Q}}\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{Q}} \{n\mapsto u(2^jn+r):1\le j\le e,\ 0\le r<2^j\}\le C \qquad(e\ge0). The alternative replaces CC by a function g(e)g(e) growing strictly slower than 2e−12^e-1, with the same quantifiers. Either assertion would contradict the lower bound of Proposition 1.6 under rationality of SS. Both assertions are false, as the following comparison shows. [uniform]

The generic assertion in Definition 3.7 is false, not a live open proposition. The 5/45/4 control in Section 10.8 has 0≤c(n)≤n0\le c(n)\le n and a tempered integral carry of rank at least 2e−12^e-1 at every depth (the unbounded-rank theorem for the rational comparison sequence, line 478). It refutes both proposed generic ceilings. A bound restricted by additional totient-specific hypotheses would be a different assertion.

Periodicity modulo vv alone does not provide the additional rank bound.

Guide to the detailed statements

The remaining sections are reference material. They restate the identities and implications in enough detail to compare their hypotheses. A repeated statement has the same meaning as before; its repetition does not supply a missing assumption.

Quantifiers and hypotheses.

The direct certificate computations cover individual parameters or a finite range. Other results hold uniformly or at arbitrarily large scales, but their conclusions are different: positivity, for example, is not nonintegrality. The finite-prefix example, rank bounds, and residue estimates must each be used only under their stated hypotheses.

Dependencies.

Sections 2 and 3 explain the principal counterexamples and sufficient conditions. The following catalogue supplies the associated formulas and source references. The later tables compare logical implications and the limits of particular estimates; their source labels are not extra mathematical hypotheses.

Series identities and finite exclusions

The identities in this section express SS through finite prefixes, scaled tails and Möbius sums. The finite calculation in Section 5.3 then excludes a specified range of rational denominators. Equivalent series representations do not by themselves extend that finite exclusion to all denominators.

The series

Definition 5.1 (The Erdős–249 constant). Let φ\varphi denote Euler’s totient function. Define S:=∑n≥1φ(n)2n=∑n:ℕφ(n)2n,S \;:=\; \sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{\varphi(n)}{2^{n}} \;=\; \sum_{n : \mathbb{N}} \frac{\varphi(n)}{2^{n}}, the two forms coinciding because φ(0)=0\varphi(0)=0; the second, ℕ\mathbb{N}-indexed form is the one carried in the Lean source. The series converges absolutely since φ(n)≤n\varphi(n)\le n. The irrationality of this value is the question under consideration.

Remark 5.2 (Status). No proof or disproof of S∉ℚS\notin\mathbb Q exists anywhere in the record, formal or informal. What exists is: one large unconditional finite denominator exclusion (§5.3), several exact reformulations of SS that relocate the same open question onto different coordinates without touching its truth value (§5.4–§5.6), and a certificate apparatus whose cofinal quantified condition is the precise open target (Definition 1.2; only its finite, checked instances are catalogued here, §5.7).

The tail-shift identity

Proposition 5.3 (Digit-shift identity). For every N:ℕN : \mathbb{N}, 2N⋅S=ΦN+RN,2^{N} \cdot S \;=\; \Phi_N + R_N, where ΦN:=∑n≤Nφ(n)⋅2N−n∈ℕ\Phi_N := \sum_{n \le N} \varphi(n) \cdot 2^{N-n} \in \mathbb{N} (the integer prefix) and RN:=∑j≥0φ(N+1+j)/2j+1R_N := \sum_{j \ge 0} \varphi(N+1+j)/2^{j+1} (the scaled tail, R{R} in Lean). [uniform] [Lean]

Consequence for rationality. Subtracting the prefix identities at N+hN+h and NN gives RN+h−RN≡2N(2h−1)S(mod⁡ℤ).R_{N+h}-R_N\equiv2^N(2^h-1)S\pmod\mathbb{Z}. If S=a/(2cv)S=a/(2^cv) with v≥1v\ge1 odd, Euler’s theorem supplies h=φ(v)>0h=\varphi(v)>0 and N0=cN_0=c, for which the difference is integral for all N≥N0N\ge N_0 (, [Lean]). Conversely, an integral difference for even one h>0,N≥0h>0,N\ge0 forces SS to be rational, because 2N(2h−1)2^N(2^h-1) is a nonzero integer. Thus the unresolved question is not this converse, but whether every such tail difference is nonintegral. Definition 1.2 expresses that question through finite residues. ◻

The finite denominator bound

The finite calculation gives a lower bound on its denominator should it happen to be rational. It is obtained by a Farey mediant argument that does not assume the quantified residue condition or use the tail-period test.

Lemma 5.4 (Farey gap, fully general). For integers a,b,c,d,r,sa,b,c,d,r,s with b>0b>0, d>0d>0, bc−ad=1bc-ad=1 (i.e. a/ba/b and c/dc/d are unimodular Farey neighbours), and as<rbas < rb, rd<csrd < cs (i.e. r/sr/s lies strictly between them): b+d≤sb+d \le s. [n/a] [Lean]

Indeed, the two strict inequalities make cs−drcs-dr and br−asbr-as positive integers, and s=b(cs−dr)+d(br−as)≥b+d,s=b(cs-dr)+d(br-as)\ge b+d, using bc−ad=1bc-ad=1. This also proves s>0s>0, which the formulation did not need to assume separately. The lemma is the classical Stern–Brocot denominator bound. The mediant (a+c)/(b+d)(a+c)/(b+d) lies between the two neighbours and is reduced: any common divisor of a+ca+c and b+db+d divides b(a+c)−a(b+d)=bc−ad=1b(a+c)-a(b+d)=bc-ad=1. It attains denominator b+db+d, so the general interval bound is sharp. A particular tail interval still requires its own endpoint and first-failure checks.

Proposition 5.5 (The Farey certificate at K=240K=240). For the window (N,K)=(1,240)(N,K)=(1,240), put V=(∑r=1240φ(1+r)2240−r)mod⁡2240.V=\left(\sum_{r=1}^{240}\varphi(1+r)2^{240-r}\right)\operatorname{mod}2^{240}. For every q:ℕq : \mathbb{N} with 0<q≤Q0:=79639646646701375323355774875831053(≈7.96×1034),0 < q \;\le\; Q_0 := 79\,639\,646\,646\,701\,375\,323\,355\,774\,875\,831\,053 \;\;(\approx 7.96\times 10^{34}), (q⋅V)mod⁡2240+243q<2240.(q \cdot V) \operatorname{mod} 2^{240} \;+\; 243\,q \;<\; 2^{240}. This bound is sharp: q=Q0+1=79639646646701375323355774875831054q = Q_0+1 = 79\,639\,646\,646\,701\,375\,323\,355\,774\,875\,831\,054 is the exact first failing denominator, obtained as the denominator of the mediant of two explicit unimodular Farey neighbours. Theorem 5.6 (Denominator exclusion). For every p∈ℚp\in\mathbb{Q} whose reduced denominator is at most Q0Q_0, S≠p.S \;\neq\; p. Equivalently: if SS is rational, its reduced denominator exceeds Q0≈7.96×1034Q_0 \approx 7.96 \times 10^{34}. [bounded] [Lean]

Remark 5.7 (What this does and does not say). Theorem 5.6 is a complete, unconditional finite fact: no rational of denominator at most Q0Q_0 equals SS. A single such bound does not exclude arbitrarily large denominators. Proving unbounded exclusions by the same mechanism would, however, establish irrationality. The docstring behind Proposition 5.5 states the question this leaves: whether sup⁡K(b+d)(K)\sup_K (b+d)(K) (the growing analogue of Q0Q_0 as the window KK grows) is unbounded as K→∞K \to \infty; which would close #249 through this theorem’s implication, entirely independently of the certificate-supply obligation of Proposition 5.3. [Open]; not claimed or proved anywhere in the record.

Each applies the finite mechanism of Lemma 5.4 and Proposition 5.5. These values do not prove that the bounds are unbounded as KK increases.

Equivalent expressions and their denominator bounds

The exact finite Farey record behind Theorem 5.6 is not tied to the φ(n)/2n\varphi(n)/2^n presentation of SS; it transfers verbatim to two other exact reformulations of the same constant, at exactly half the bound. Amiram Eldar posted both reformulations to OEIS A256936 on 15 March 2026: an equivalent coprimality interpretation of Proposition 5.9 in revision 28, and the Möbius-square formula of Proposition 5.14 in revision 31 . Steve Fan posted the Möbius-square formula on the problem’s forum thread on 16 May 2026 [7]. Both identities follow here from Möbius inversion and geometric sums, with the proofs recorded in the linked declarations.

Proposition 5.9 (Fair-coin coprimality form). Let X,YX,Y be independent random variables with Pr⁡(X=n)=Pr⁡(Y=n)=2−n\Pr(X=n)=\Pr(Y=n)=2^{-n} for n≥1n \ge 1 (independent fair-coin waiting times). Then S=12+Pr⁡(gcd⁡(X,Y)=1)=12+∑a,b≥1gcd⁡(a,b)=12−(a+b).S \;=\; \tfrac12 \;+\; \Pr\bigl(\gcd(X,Y)=1\bigr) \;=\; \tfrac12 \;+\; \sum_{\substack{a,b\ge 1\\ \gcd(a,b)=1}} 2^{-(a+b)}. Equivalently, on the visible lattice: summing 2−(a+b)2^{-(a+b)} over the half-open coprime pairs (a≥1a\ge1, b≥0b\ge0, gcd⁡(a,b)=1\gcd(a,b)=1) recovers ∑nφ(n)/2n\sum_n \varphi(n)/2^n exactly, with no boundary correction, because the visible-point count on the half-open antidiagonal at height nn equals φ(n)\varphi(n) for every nn, including n=0,1n=0,1. [n/a] [Lean]

Proposition 5.10 (The gcd-layer normalisation). For independent fair-coin waiting times as above, ∑g≥1Pr⁡(gcd⁡(X,Y)=g)=1\sum_{g\ge1}\Pr(\gcd(X,Y)=g)=1 exactly; and for every d>0d>0, Pr⁡(d∣X∧d∣Y)=1/(2d−1)2\Pr(d\mid X \wedge d\mid Y) = 1/(2^d-1)^2. [uniform] [Lean]

With Q1Q_1 as in Theorem 5.11: for every a∈ℤa\in\mathbb{Z}, d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} with 0<d≤Q10<d\le Q_1, the signed series T:=∑m≥1μ(m)/(2m−1)2=S−12T := \sum_{m\ge1} \mu(m)/(2^m-1)^2 = S - \tfrac12 (see §5.5) is not equal to a/da/d. Remark 5.13 (Why the bound halves, and why this is not new information). Q1=⌊Q0/2⌋Q_1 = \lfloor Q_0/2 \rfloor arithmetically: Q0Q_0 is odd (Q0=79639646646701375323355774875831053Q_0 = 79\,639\,646\,646\,701\,375\,323\,355\,774\,875\,831\,053), so Q0/2=39819823323350687661677887437915526.5Q_0/2 = 39\,819\,823\,323\,350\,687\,661\,677\,887\,437\,915\,526.5 and Q1Q_1 is its floor. The Möbius-weighted identity

Proposition 5.14 (Möbius-square reduction). S=∑n≥1φ(n)2n=12+∑d≥1μ(d)(2d−1)2,S \;=\; \sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\varphi(n)}{2^n} \;=\; \frac12 \;+\; \sum_{d\ge1}\frac{\mu(d)}{(2^d-1)^2}, where μ\mu is the Möbius function, so μ(d)∈{−1,0,1}\mu(d)\in\{-1,0,1\} for every dd. Consequently Erdős #249 ⇔\iff T:=∑d≥1μ(d)/(2d−1)2∉ℚT:=\sum_{d\ge1}\mu(d)/(2^d-1)^2 \notin \mathbb{Q}, since adding a rational number does not change irrationality. [n/a] [Lean]

Remark 5.15 (Why the bounded coefficients matter; the Erdős-1948 regime). The identity of Proposition 5.14 rewrites SS (equivalently TT) as a Lambert-type series with squared denominators and bounded Möbius weights. To see the constant 1/21/2 directly, expand ∑d≥1μ(d)2d−1=∑n≥1∑d∣nμ(d)2n=12.\sum_{d\ge1}\frac{\mu(d)}{2^d-1} =\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)}{2^n}=\frac12. Combining this identity with φ=μ*Id\varphi=\mu*\mathrm{Id} and 2d=(2d−1)+12^d=(2^d-1)+1 proves the formula for TT; absolute convergence justifies the rearrangements. Thus the corresponding first-power sum L(μ):=∑dμ(d)/(2d−1)L(\mu):=\sum_d\mu(d)/(2^d-1) is rational, whereas L(1)=∑d≥11/(2d−1)=EL(1)=\sum_{d\ge1}1/(2^d-1)=E is the Erdős–Borwein constant. Erdős proved its irrationality in 1948 [9] and the supplied formal source also proves it irrational (, [Lean]).

In contrast, the coefficients of the original power series satisfy 0≤φ(n)≤n0\le\varphi(n)\le n and are unbounded. Bounded Möbius weights do not make the new denominators powers of a fixed base, so they do not turn this representation into a bounded-digit expansion. The function φ\varphi has average order 6n/π26n/\pi^2, equivalently ∑k≤xφ(k)∼3x2/π2\sum_{k\le x}\varphi(k)\sim 3x^2/\pi^2, but there is no pointwise estimate φ(n)=Θ(n)\varphi(n)=\Theta(n). The near-integer irrationality criterion (formalised generically as and its base-power specialisation , both [Lean]) applies to either representation if its nonzero approximation errors can be established. Boundedness of the coefficients does not itself establish those errors. Erdős’s 1948 argument is itself a proof for the specific Lambert series: it chooses arguments by a system of congruences so that the divisor counts along a block are divisible by increasing powers of the base, and a tail bound then forces a long run of zero digits . Boundedness of a signed weight supplies none of that divisibility input.

The rational identity L(μ)=1/2L(\mu)=1/2 is already a warning: bounded signed coefficients alone do not imply irrationality. The later denominator calculations retain the Möbius terms whose indices do not divide the chosen LCM; those terms cannot be discarded when transferring an estimate.

A general squared-Lambert identity

Proposition 5.16 (The squared-Lambert identity). For w:ℕ→ℝw:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R} with |w(d)|≤d|w(d)|\le d for all d>0d>0, and 0≤r<10\le r<1: ∑d≥1w(d)(rd1−rd)2=∑n≥1(∑e∣nw(e)(ne−1))rn.\sum_{d\ge1} w(d)\left(\frac{r^d}{1-r^d}\right)^2 \;=\; \sum_{n\ge1}\left(\sum_{e\mid n} w(e)\Bigl(\tfrac{n}{e}-1\Bigr)\right) r^n. [uniform] [Lean]

The identity follows by expanding rd/(1−rd)r^d/(1-r^d) as a geometric series and interchanging absolutely convergent sums. It is the squared analogue of the classical divisor-sum Lambert identity ∑nanqn/(1−qn)=∑m(∑d∣mad)qm\sum_na_nq^n/(1-q^n)=\sum_m\bigl(\sum_{d\mid m}a_d\bigr)q^m .

At r=1/2r=1/2, the choices w=1w=1 and w=φw=\varphi give the following two identities. They help distinguish the role of the weight from that of the squared denominator.

Proposition 5.17 (The divisor-sum identity). ∑d≥11(2d−1)2=∑n≥1σ(n)−τ(n)2n=ζq(2)−ζq(1) at q=12,\sum_{d\ge1} \frac{1}{(2^d-1)^2} \;=\; \sum_{n\ge1} \frac{\sigma(n)-\tau(n)}{2^n} \;=\; \zeta_q(2)-\zeta_q(1) \text{ at } q=\tfrac12, where σ\sigma is the sum-of-divisors function and τ\tau the number-of-divisors function. The identity is machine-checked ([Lean]). With ζq(s)=∑n≥1ns−1qn/(1−qn)\zeta_q(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{s-1}q^n/(1-q^n), Postelmans and Van Assche prove that 1,ζq(1),ζq(2)1,\zeta_q(1),\zeta_q(2) are linearly independent over ℚ\mathbb{Q} for q=1/pq=1/p with an integer p≥2p\ge2 ; at q=12q=\tfrac12 this gives the irrationality of the value ζq(2)−ζq(1)\zeta_q(2)-\zeta_q(1) ([Cited], not formalised in this corpus). Two irrational numbers can have a rational difference, so the separate irrationality of the two values would not suffice. [n/a]

Remark 5.19 (Related series). Writing L(f):=∑df(d)/(2d−1)L(f):=\sum_d f(d)/(2^d-1) and L2(f):=∑df(d)/(2d−1)2L_2(f):=\sum_d f(d)/(2^d-1)^2, the preceding identities give L(μ)=12L(\mu)=\tfrac12 (rational), L(1)=EL(1)=E (Erdős–Borwein, irrational, [Lean]), L(φ)=2L(\varphi)=2 (rational); L2(μ)=S−12L_2(\mu)=S-\tfrac12 ([Open], this is #249), L2(1)=ζq(2)−ζq(1)L_2(1)=\zeta_q(2)-\zeta_q(1) ([Cited] irrational, Proposition 5.17), L2(φ)=𝔼[gcd⁡(X,Y)]L_2(\varphi)=\mathbb{E}[\gcd(X,Y)] ([Open], Proposition 5.18). Detailed statements

The following statements collect the dependencies used in the earlier arguments. We begin with unconditional identities, rank bounds and finite examples. The next subsection supplies the definitions and elementary implications, followed by the quantified conditions that would be needed to prove irrationality. A source link supports the indicated statement, not an unproved hypothesis appearing in it.

Unconditional structure and finite examples

The distinction between a finite example and a family at arbitrarily large scales is important here. The rank and denominator statements below hold with their displayed quantifiers; the residue computations establish only the explicitly stated finite ranges.

Theorem 6.1 (Rationality gives an eventual tail period). If S=a/(2cv)S=a/(2^cv) with a∈ℤa\in\mathbb Z, c∈ℕc\in\mathbb N and vv a positive odd integer, then RN+h−RN∈ℤ(N≥c),h=φ(v)>0.R_{N+h}-R_N\in\mathbb Z\qquad(N\ge c),\qquad h=\varphi(v)>0. Euler’s theorem gives v∣2h−1v\mid2^h-1, and the prefix-tail identity then makes 2N(2h−1)S2^N(2^h-1)S integral. Thus rationality supplies a positive shift for which all sufficiently late tail differences are integral.

If S∈ℚS\in\mathbb Q, there are an integer v>0v>0 and an integer sequence uu such that u(N+1)=2u(N)−vφ(N+1),u(N)/2N→0,u(N+1)=2u(N)-v\varphi(N+1),\qquad u(N)/2^N\longrightarrow0, and, for every e≥0e\ge0, the sequences n↦u(2jn+r)n\mapsto u(2^jn+r) with 1≤j≤e1\le j\le e and 0≤r<2j0\le r<2^j span a space of ℚ\mathbb Q-dimension at least 2e−12^e-1.

The formal term tempered means exactly u(N)/2N→0u(N)/2^N\to0 here, not a separate assumption of subexponential growth. This rank lower bound is a necessary consequence of rationality, not a contradiction. An upper bound using additional properties of the actual totient coefficients would be needed; the later rational comparison rules out such a bound for arbitrary rational coefficient series.

Theorem 6.3 (Independence of the retained dyadic sections). For every integer e≥0e\ge0, the family φ(n),φ(2n),φ(2jn+r)(1≤j≤e,0<r<2j,r odd)\varphi(n),\quad\varphi(2n),\quad \varphi(2^jn+r)\quad(1\le j\le e,\ 0<r<2^j,\ r\text{ odd}) is linearly independent over ℚ\mathbb Q and has 2e+12^e+1 members. At e=0e=0 this family still contains φ(2n)\varphi(2n); it is not the full level-zero truncation, which consists only of φ(n)\varphi(n). For e≥1e\ge1 it is the basis of the full truncated dyadic family.

The proof separates one section at a time: the Chinese remainder theorem forces suitable prime divisors in the other affine arguments, while Dirichlet’s theorem makes the selected argument prime. This proves independence, not just the displayed cardinality. In particular, the span of all dyadic sections is infinite-dimensional; that conclusion alone says nothing about rationality of their weighted sum.

Definitions and elementary identities

The finite test rests on two identities: the prefix-tail decomposition and the truncation of a tail difference. We state those first, then give the soundness and completeness arguments, the LCM specialisation and the corresponding rational-approximation criteria. The subsequent Möbius identities describe the same series with different coefficient weights.

Initial implications

Definition 6.13 (The scaled tail). For N∈ℕN\in\mathbb N, RN=∑j≥0φ(N+1+j)2j+1.R_N=\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{\varphi(N+1+j)}{2^{j+1}}. The series converges because φ(n)≤n\varphi(n)\le n. It is the tail of SS multiplied by 2N2^N, not the fractional part of 2NS2^NS; indeed, RNR_N need not lie in [0,1)[0,1).

Definition 6.14 (The truncated tail difference). For h,N,L∈ℕh,N,L\in\mathbb{N}, define the integer D(h,N,L)=∑j=0L−1(φ(N+h+1+j)−φ(N+1+j))2L−1−j.D(h,N,L)=\sum_{j=0}^{L-1} \bigl(\varphi(N+h+1+j)-\varphi(N+1+j)\bigr)2^{L-1-j}. The sum is empty when L=0L=0. Dividing it by 2L2^L gives the first LL terms of RN+h−RNR_{N+h}-R_N. Computing the finitely many totients therefore determines D(h,N,L)D(h,N,L) exactly; the residue inequality below is the decidable condition.

[n/a]

Definition 6.15 (The central-residue inequality). For h,N,L∈ℕh,N,L\in\mathbb N, the finite condition 𝒞(h,N,L)\mathcal C(h,N,L) is N+h+L+2<D(h,N,L)mod⁡2L<2L−(N+h+L+2).N+h+L+2<D(h,N,L)\operatorname{mod}2^L<2^L-(N+h+L+2). It puts the residue outside both endpoint intervals of width N+h+L+2N+h+L+2. After division by 2L2^L, the excluded width tends to zero as LL grows with h,Nh,N fixed. No analytic hypothesis is part of this finite test; the separate condition Sep\mathrm{Sep} quantifies over such tests.

Proposition 6.16 (The prefix-tail identity). For every N∈ℕN\in\mathbb N, 2NS=ΦN+RN,ΦN=∑n≤Nφ(n)2N−n∈ℤ.2^NS=\Phi_N+R_N, \qquad \Phi_N=\sum_{n\le N}\varphi(n)2^{N-n}\in\mathbb Z. Thus RNR_N and 2NS2^NS have the same fractional part. Subtracting the identities at N+hN+h and NN gives the tail-difference congruence used in the irrationality criterion.

Proposition 6.21 (The Farey gap lemma). Let a,b,c,d,r,s∈ℤa,b,c,d,r,s\in\mathbb Z, with b,d>0b,d>0 and bc−ad=1bc-ad=1. If as<rbandrd<cs,as<rb\quad\text{and}\quad rd<cs, then b+d≤sb+d\le s. The two cross-products rb−asrb-as and cs−rdcs-rd are positive integers, and s=d(rb−as)+b(cs−rd)≥d+b.s=d(rb-as)+b(cs-rd)\ge d+b. Proposition 6.22 (An irrationality criterion from rational approximations). Let x∈ℝx\in\mathbb R and let uk=pk/qk∈ℚu_k=p_k/q_k\in\mathbb Q be in lowest terms, with qk>0q_k>0. Indeed, if x=a/bx=a/b with a∈ℤa\in\mathbb Z and b≥1b\ge1, a nonzero integer numerator gives qk|x−uk|=|aqk−bpk|/b≥1/bq_k|x-u_k|=|a q_k-b p_k|/b\ge1/b, a contradiction. This elementary criterion requires both nonvanishing and the scaled error estimate. Convergence uk→xu_k\to x alone is insufficient, and the approximants need not be continued-fraction convergents.

Proposition 6.23 (An irrationality criterion from near integers). Let ξ∈ℝ\xi\in\mathbb R. Suppose that for every integer q≥1q\ge1 there are integers m,zm,z with 0<|mξ−z|<1/q.0<|m\xi-z|<1/q. Then ξ\xi is irrational: if ξ=a/b\xi=a/b with b≥1b\ge1, every nonzero such difference is at least 1/b1/b. The strict lower bound excludes exact integer hits; the upper bound must be available for arbitrarily large qq.

For a binary example, form a number by concatenating the blocks 1010 at square indices k≥1k\ge1 and 0101 at the other indices. Its binary expansion is not eventually periodic, since the block sequence has increasingly long gaps between the square indices, so the number is irrational. There are no three consecutive equal digits. Every fractional part after a binary shift therefore lies in [1/8,7/8][1/8,7/8], and the multiples 2nξ2^n\xi do not approach the integers. Equivalent quantified certificate conditions

Each statement in this block relates a quantified certificate condition to irrationality. The implications are proved; the assertions that certificates occur beyond every threshold remain unproved. Completeness gives equivalences for the base condition and the LCM-diagonal condition. The one-directional implications remain useful proof components, but do not by themselves describe the full logical relation.

Theorem 6.47 (The quantified certificate condition is equivalent to irrationality). (∀h:ℕ,0<h→∀N0:ℕ,∃N≥N0,∃L,𝒞(h,N,L))↔S∉ℚ\big(\forall h:\mathbb{N},\ 0<h \to \forall N_0:\mathbb{N},\ \exists N\ge N_0,\ \exists L,\ \mathcal{C}(h,N,L)\big) \leftrightarrow S\notin\mathbb Q. The quantified-condition side is exactly 𝒞(h,N,L)\mathcal{C}(h,N,L) quantified as ∀h≥1∀N0≥0∃N≥N0∃L\forall h\ge1\ \forall N_0\ge0\ \exists N\ge N_0\ \exists L. The universally quantified assertion remains unproved. The equivalence identifies the finite witnesses that suffice; it does not establish their existence beyond every threshold.

For fixed h,N∈ℕh,N\in\mathbb{N}, a depth L∈ℕL\in\mathbb{N} satisfying N+L+2≤D(h,N,L)mod⁡2L≤2L−(N+h+L+2)N+L+2\ \le\ D(h,N,L)\operatorname{mod}2^L \ \le\ 2^L-(N+h+L+2) exists if and only if RN+h−RN∉ℤR_{N+h}-R_N\notin\mathbb Z. The endpoint inequalities are non-strict.

Proof. The exact truncation identity leaves an error RN+h+L−RN+LR_{N+h+L}-R_{N+L} strictly between −(N+L+2)-(N+L+2) and N+h+L+2N+h+L+2. An integral tail difference would therefore put the residue in [0,N+L+2)[0,N+L+2) or (2L−(N+h+L+2),2L)(2^L-(N+h+L+2),2^L), contrary to the displayed test. Conversely, a nonintegral difference has a symmetric certificate by Theorem 6.19, and every symmetric certificate satisfies this wider interval condition. ◻

At H3=6H_3=6 and L=6L=6, the discrepancy is D(6,6,6)=270D(6,6,6)=270, with residue 1414 modulo 6464. The directed interval is [14,44][14,44], so its lower endpoint succeeds. The symmetric interval is (20,44)(20,44) and fails; its first successful depth is 77. Thus the wider test can improve the first successful depth, but no uniform depth saving is asserted. Replacing 𝒞\mathcal C by the displayed inequality in Theorem 6.49 gives the equivalent directed diagonal condition, whose occurrence at arbitrarily large scales remains unproved.  [Lean]

Proposition 6.76 (The lower bound and a false proposed upper bound). By Prop. 6.98, the canonical dyadic totient-kernel family is unconditionally (2e+1)(2^e+1)-dimensional at every level e≥1e\ge1. Rationality of SS forces an associated tempered carry orbit with ℚ\mathbb Q-rank ≥2e−1\ge 2^e-1 at every level (Prop. 6.90). An upper bound independent of ee for these same carry ranks would contradict the lower bound. More generally, a bound g(e)g(e) with g(e)<2e−1g(e)<2^e-1 at some level e≥1e\ge1 would suffice, provided it applies to the actual carry under the hypothetical rationality of SS. A bound that merely grows with ee need not contradict anything. The generic assertion for arbitrary rational coefficient series is false: the 5/45/4 comparison sequence in Section 10.8 has an integer carry satisfying the growth condition and the same rank lower bound. The incompatible integer identity and the finite-shift counterexample (Observation 6.115) remain separate counterexample results. None is a generic rationality-driven rank ceiling. The evidence label below applies to the proved rank floor and counterexample results, not to the counterfactual upper bound. [uniform] [Lean]

An integral tail difference would give one of the initial candidates and would remain in the open strip |ch,N,z(i)|<N+i+h+2|c_{h,N,z}(i)|<N+i+h+2 at every step. Equality at a boundary already excludes a candidate. This is the soundness implication for a specified finite test; no bound for a successful search depth is asserted.

Further exact identities

The identities in this subsection hold independently of the proposed residue tests. Each gives either an exact expression or a bound that can be used when studying those tests.

Proposition 6.78 (The exact totient difference on an LCM progression). Put H=H(t)H=H(t). For a divisor j∣Hj\mid H, this assertion contains a useful product formula, not merely a change of notation. Set a=H/j,g1=gcd⁡(j,a+1),g2=gcd⁡(j,2a+1).a=H/j,\qquad g_1=\gcd(j,a+1),\qquad g_2=\gcd(j,2a+1). Then δt(j)=φ(j)(g2φ(2a+1)φ(g2)−g1φ(a+1)φ(g1)).\delta_t(j)=\varphi(j)\left( \frac{g_2\varphi(2a+1)}{\varphi(g_2)} -\frac{g_1\varphi(a+1)}{\varphi(g_1)}\right). Here j≥1j\ge1 because H>0H>0, so both denominators are nonzero. The identity follows from φ(jx)=φ(j)φ(x)gcd⁡(j,x)/φ(gcd⁡(j,x))\varphi(jx)=\varphi(j)\varphi(x)\gcd(j,x)/\varphi(\gcd(j,x)), which retains all primes shared by jj and xx. If every prime dividing jj also divides aa, then g1=g2=1g_1=g_2=1, and the formula reduces to φ(j)(φ(2a+1)−φ(a+1))\varphi(j)\bigl(\varphi(2a+1)-\varphi(a+1)\bigr). For example, at H=j=2H=j=2 the two gcds are g1=2g_1=2 and g2=1g_2=1; the exact difference is φ(6)−φ(4)=0\varphi(6)-\varphi(4)=0, whereas discarding the gcd factors would give 11. Proposition 6.90 (A consequence of rationality and its limitation). If S∈ℚS\in\mathbb Q, there are a positive integer vv and a tempered integer carry orbit uu such that its retained sections through every level ee have rational rank at least 2e−12^e-1. At the same time, those sections are uniformly eventually periodic modulo vv. Periodicity after reduction modulo vv is a statement in a finite quotient; it is not a rank upper bound over ℚ\mathbb Q. Proposition 6.76 gives the lower bound, while the rational comparison sequence explains why a general rank upper bound cannot be deduced from these recurrence assumptions alone. [uniform] [Lean]

This progression is reduced: its residue is odd and is −H≢0(mod⁡r)-H\not\equiv0\pmod r. Then p≡3(mod⁡4)p\equiv3\pmod4, so φ(p)=p−1≡2(mod⁡4)\varphi(p)=p-1\equiv2\pmod4, whereas r∣p+Hr\mid p+H gives 4∣φ(p+H)4\mid\varphi(p+H). Subtracting gives the stated congruence. This supplies the arithmetic congruence at arbitrarily large primes; the additional finite exclusion in Proposition 6.70 remains a separate hypothesis.

Counterexamples and limitations

Each example below is a counterexample to a stated deduction, not to irrationality of SS. The assumptions that fail to suffice are given with the example, so that its conclusion is not extended to other arguments.

Observation 6.106 (The sign of the actual endpoint representative). Assume a≥8a\ge8, H=H2aH=H_{2^a} and J+K+a+6<2⋅2aJ+K+a+6<2\cdot2^a, as in Proposition 6.84. If d=R2H+J−RH+Jd=R_{2H+J}-R_{H+J} is an integer, define c0=d,cj+1=2cj−(φ(2H+J+j+1)−φ(H+J+j+1)).c_0=d,\qquad c_{j+1}=2c_j-\bigl(\varphi(2H+J+j+1)-\varphi(H+J+j+1)\bigr). The tail recurrence gives cK=R2H+J+K−RH+J+K>0c_K=R_{2H+J+K}-R_{H+J+K}>0. Its negative is an integer representative satisfying |−cK|≤2H+J+K+2,−cK≡D(H,H+J,K)(mod⁡2K).|{-c_K}|\le2H+J+K+2,\qquad -c_K\equiv D(H,H+J,K)\pmod{2^K}. Thus the representative corresponding to the actual tail is negative. The stated size bound allows it to remain in the endpoint interval, so its sign alone does not contradict integrality. Other integers in that interval with the same residue need not represent the actual tail. Proposition 6.85 gives the further residue separation that would exclude this case. [uniform] [Lean]

Observation 6.109 (A rational sequence with matching parity).

Start with the coefficient sequence 0,1,1,2,4,4,4,…0,1,1,2,4,4,4,\ldots, indexed from 00. For each m=2k+3m=2^{k+3}, k≥0k\ge0, replace the pair at positions m,m+1m,m+1 from (4,4)(4,4) to (6,0)(6,0), leaving all other coefficients unchanged. These pairs are disjoint. It is not eventually periodic, since the gaps between its occurrences of 66 tend to infinity. This construction uses the particular initial parity pattern and the binary weights; it does not establish an analogous result for arbitrary prescribed parities or other summand weights. Observation 6.110 (What the parity example disproves). Observation 6.114 (The prime-power restriction in the unit-gap refinement). The ordinary interval test excludes a rational denominator when its possible numerator interval contains no integer. Reduced fractions permit a refinement: every numerator is coprime to its denominator, so an interval containing only nonunits can also be excluded. For a candidate S=a/(2cu)S=a/(2^c u) in lowest terms, with u>0u>0 odd and N≥cN\ge c, the integer uRN=2N−ca−uΦNuR_N=2^{N-c}a-u\Phi_N is coprime to uu. Its possible integer values are therefore J+1,…,J+LJ+1,\ldots,J+L. The refined condition is gcd⁡(J+t,u)>1\gcd(J+t,u)>1 for all 1≤t≤L1\le t\le L, contradicting the required coprimality of uRNuR_N. For a prime pp and e≥1e\ge1, nonunits modulo pep^e are exactly the multiples of pp. Since two consecutive integers cannot both be multiples of pp, the condition for u=peu=p^e is equivalent to L=0orL=1 and p∣J+1.L=0\quad\text{or}\quad L=1\text{ and }p\mid J+1. Thus a successful refined certificate at a prime-power denominator has at most one candidate integer. This is not a bound for an arbitrary window: (u,N,K)=(3,3,3)(u,N,K)=(3,3,3) gives V=2V=2, J=0J=0, W=6W=6 and L=3L=3, and the test fails because 1,2,31,2,3 are not all nonunits modulo 33. The prime-power restriction also matters. With the actual totient window (u,N,K)=(15,13,8)(u,N,K)=(15,13,8), one gets V=148,J=8,W=172,L=2.V=148,\quad J=8,\quad W=172,\quad L=2. Observation 6.116 (Compatible carries for fixed-precision local symbols). For example, prescribing an odd coefficient modulo 88 permits any coefficient of the form a+8za+8z with aa odd and z∈ℤz\in\mathbb Z. Whatever the incoming integer carry ee, one can choose zz so that 2e+a+8z2e+a+8z lies between −4-4 and 33. More generally, fix u≥1u\ge1 and a finite list of integers vj≥0v_j\ge0 and odd integers aja_j. Starting from any integer e0e_0, there are integers zjz_j and coefficients cj=2vj(aj+2uzj),ej+1=2ej+cj,|ej+1|≤2vj+u−1.c_j=2^{v_j}(a_j+2^u z_j),\qquad e_{j+1}=2e_j+c_j, \qquad |e_{j+1}|\le2^{v_j+u-1}. At each step, reduce 2ej+2vjaj2e_j+2^{v_j}a_j to its centred representative modulo 2vj+u2^{v_j+u}, choosing the interval [−2vj+u−1,2vj+u−1).[-2^{v_j+u-1},2^{v_j+u-1}). Solving for zjz_j gives the stated next carry. Iterate this choice. The bounds apply to the resulting states, not to the arbitrary initial state e0e_0. The unrestricted higher quotients zjz_j are essential: the construction prescribes a valuation and a finite unit residue, not the full coefficients or their signs. It therefore does not realise a prescribed totient-difference sequence. Observation 6.117 (Correction-free factorisation does not ensure nonvanishing). Consider the two finite differences φ(65)−φ(65)=0,φ(78)−φ(70)=24−24=0.\varphi(65)-\varphi(65)=0,\qquad \varphi(78)-\varphi(70)=24-24=0. They arise from the square-congruence choice 52≡52(mod⁡132)52\equiv52\pmod{13^2} and 52≡2(mod⁡52)52\equiv2\pmod{5^2}. The four arguments factor as 13⋅513\cdot5, 5⋅135\cdot13, 13⋅613\cdot6 and 5⋅145\cdot14; in each product the prime and cofactor are coprime. Thus all four totients have the correction-free form φ(pm)=(p−1)φ(m)\varphi(pm)=(p-1)\varphi(m), yet both differences vanish. Nonvanishing is also possible: the choices 27≡0(mod⁡32)27\equiv0\pmod{3^2} and 27≡2(mod⁡52)27\equiv2\pmod{5^2} give φ(30)−φ(30)=0,φ(33)−φ(35)=20−24=−4,\varphi(30)-\varphi(30)=0,\qquad \varphi(33)-\varphi(35)=20-24=-4, again with coprime factors at every term. The square-CRT construction removes the non-coprime multiplicativity correction on the prescribed finite range. That property alone does not imply nonvanishing. These are explicit witnesses of the two possibilities, not a claim that the first is a smallest counterexample. [n/a] [Lean (docstring-sourced)] 

Observation 6.118 (No fixed integer clears every primitive denominator). Let A=φ*μA=\varphi*\mu be the Dirichlet convolution used in Proposition 6.102. At prime powers, A(p)=p−2,A(pr)=pr−2(p−1)2(r≥2).A(p)=p-2,\qquad A(p^r)=p^{r-2}(p-1)^2\quad(r\ge2). These follow by subtracting consecutive prime-power values of φ\varphi. For every odd prime pp, the reduced denominator of A(p)/pA(p)/p is pp. For every prime pp, the reduced denominator of A(p2)/p2A(p^2)/p^2 is p2p^2, including the denominator 44 at p=2p=2. Consequently any positive integer DD for which DA(n)/n∈ℤDA(n)/n\in\mathbb Z for all 1≤n≤N1\le n\le N must be divisible by every odd prime p≤Np\le N, every prime square p2≤Np^2\le N, and by 44 once N≥4N\ge4. No fixed DD can do this for all nn, since there are infinitely many odd primes. In periodic-point counting, the quantities A(n)/nA(n)/n would count orbits of length nn; their integrality and nonnegativity characterise realisable periodic-point sequences [26]. Here only the denominator obstruction is used. It excludes a fixed integer clearing all these particular coordinates, not every possible Euler-product representation or an argument with a multiplier growing with NN. It is not an irrationality proof for SS. [n/a] [Lean] 

Observation 6.119 (A finite exclusion is not a membership test). A successful residue certificate proves the exclusion stated in its soundness theorem. Failure of that sufficient condition at finitely many depths does not prove integrality of the tail difference. In particular, a finite unsuccessful search cannot be substituted for the eventual-period assertion needed to prove rationality. The same logical distinction occurs for the linked greedy test in a separate Mersenne achievement-set problem: its finite inequality implies nonmembership. The linked object is a definition, with a soundness theorem in the same file, not a theorem asserting a universal impossibility of finite rationality proofs for Problem #249. Membership or rationality established by some additional exact identity is not excluded by this observation. Likewise, the successful finite ranges in Propositions 6.94 and 6.104 remain finite ranges until an unbounded supply is proved. [n/a] [Math; related Lean definition] 

Related structural results

The following results concern the Möbius-weighted series, integer carry recurrences, rational approximations, and factorizations used above. Each statement retains its pinned formal-source reference. The statements are grouped by their mathematical objects, rather than by the order in which files were added to the repository.

Log-concavity of the Möbius-weighted series

The series Θr=∑n≥0μ(n+1)/(2n+1−1)r\Theta_r=\sum_{n\ge0}\mu(n+1)/(2^{n+1}-1)^r includes S−1/2S-1/2 at r=2r=2. The next result proves strict log-concavity for every integer r≥1r\ge1. This is an order property of these values, not an irrationality criterion.

Definition 6.120. For each integer r≥1r\ge1, put Θr=∑n≥0μ(n+1)(2n+1−1)r=1−3−r+∑n≥0μ(n+3)(2n+3−1)r.\Theta_r=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{\mu(n+1)}{(2^{n+1}-1)^r} =1-3^{-r}+\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{\mu(n+3)}{(2^{n+3}-1)^r}. The first two summands isolate the dominant contribution. The remaining absolute sum is at most 1/(2r(2r−1))1/(2^r(2^r-1)), by comparison with ∑n≥22−rn\sum_{n\ge2}2^{-rn}. In particular, Θr>0\Theta_r>0 for r≥1r\ge1: 1−3−r≥2/31-3^{-r}\ge2/3 and this tail bound is at most 1/21/2. .

Theorem 6.121 (The values at exponents one and two). The first two values are Θ1=1/2\Theta_1=1/2 and Θ2=S−1/2\Theta_2=S-1/2. .

Observation 6.124. The inequality excludes a representation Θr=∫0∞xrdν(x)\Theta_r=\int_0^\infty x^r\,d\nu(x) by a positive measure with these finite moments: Cauchy–Schwarz would give Θr+12≤ΘrΘr+2\Theta_{r+1}^2\le\Theta_r\Theta_{r+2}. It does not by itself imply irrationality of Θ2\Theta_2. Indeed, the rational sequence 1−3−r1-3^{-r} satisfies the same strict log-concavity inequalities. Thus the determinant sign supplies an obstruction to a positive-moment representation, not a rational-approximation estimate.

The accompanying formal results include a rectangular determinant expansion derived from the Leibniz formula (, [Lean], [uniform], ), and the following elementary parity fact: in a finite sum of dyadic fractions, if the largest denominator exponent occurs once and its numerator is odd, clearing that denominator gives an odd numerator (, [Lean], [uniform], ).

Integer recurrences and rational binary series

For a binary series with integer coefficients, rationality can be expressed by an integer recurrence whose growth is smaller than 2N2^N. The next equivalence is elementary algebra and convergence; no novelty is claimed for it.

Theorem 6.125 (Integer recurrence criterion for a binary series). Let c:ℕ→ℕc:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} satisfy c(n)≤nc(n)\le n. Then ∑n≥1c(n)2−n\sum_{n\ge1}c(n)2^{-n} is rational if and only if there are an integer v>0v>0 and an integer sequence uu such that u(N+1)=2u(N)−vc(N+1),u(N)2N→0.u(N+1)=2u(N)-v\,c(N+1),\qquad \frac{u(N)}{2^N}\longrightarrow0. For each fixed vv, such a sequence is unique and equals u(N)=vRNc,RNc=∑j≥1c(N+j)2j.u(N)=vR^c_N,\qquad R^c_N=\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{c(N+j)}{2^j}. .

Proof. Iterating the recurrence gives the finite identity u(N)2N=u(0)−v∑n=1Nc(n)2n.\frac{u(N)}{2^N}=u(0)-v\sum_{n=1}^N\frac{c(n)}{2^n}. The boundary condition therefore forces the series to equal u(0)/vu(0)/v; subtracting the prefix gives u(N)=vRNcu(N)=vR^c_N. Conversely, when the series is rational, choose an integer v>0v>0 making its product with vv an integer, use this product as u(0)u(0), and iterate the recurrence. The displayed identity identifies the resulting integer sequence with vRNcvR^c_N. Since 0≤RNc≤N+20\le R^c_N\le N+2, its ratio to 2N2^N tends to zero. ◻

Without the boundary condition, any integer u(0)u(0) gives an integer solution of the recurrence, whether the series is rational or irrational. Two solutions with the same vv differ by 2N2^N times their initial difference. Thus the limit, not the recurrence alone, determines the initial value. Changing vv rescales the canonical solution; uniqueness is asserted only for a fixed multiplier.

Proposition 6.126 (Uniqueness under the growth condition). A real sequence dd with d(N+1)=2d(N)d(N{+}1)=2d(N) and d(N)=o(2N)d(N)=o(2^N) is identically zero. .

Observation 6.127 (The specified finite-state decoder is impossible). Fix m≥2m\ge2, put R=⌊(m+1)/2⌋R=\lfloor(m+1)/2\rfloor, and for 0≤r≤R0\le r\le R define cm,r(n)={R−r,n=m,2r,n=m+1,0,otherwise.c_{m,r}(n)= \begin{cases} R-r,&n=m,\\ 2r,&n=m+1,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases} The two nonzero terms have total contribution (R−r)2−m+2r2−(m+1)=R2−m(R-r)2^{-m}+2r2^{-(m+1)}=R2^{-m}, independent of rr. All coefficients and scaled tails before mm are therefore the same, whereas the scaled tail at mm is rr. No map from a state common to this whole family can recover that tail. More generally, exact recovery of all its possible values requires at least R+1R+1 distinct labels. . The sequences in this family have identical histories before the isolated change but different subsequent tails. Therefore that finite history alone cannot determine the exact tail in this class of sequences. This is not a conclusion about the totient sequence.

There is also an infinite family with a common rational value. Let a:ℕ→{0,1}a:\mathbb{N}\to\{0,1\} satisfy a(0)=0a(0)=0, and put c(2k)=k−a(k)c(2k)=k-a(k) and c(2k+1)=2a(k)c(2k+1)=2a(k). The adjacent terms contribute k4−kk4^{-k}, so ∑n≥1c(n)2n=∑k≥1k4k=49,\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{c(n)}{2^n} =\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{k}{4^k}=\frac49, regardless of the binary sequence aa. The cited result also gives an integer recurrence satisfying the growth condition (, [Lean], [uniform], ). The assumptions a(0)=0a(0)=0 and a(k)∈{0,1}a(k)\in\{0,1\} are part of that formal statement, not an arbitrary bounded-input hypothesis. For comparison, the identity coefficients c(n)=nc(n)=n have the explicit multiplier-one recurrence u(N)=N+2u(N)=N+2 (, [Lean], [fixed], ).

Rational approximation with a squared-Mersenne remainder

The first-order Lambert term in the diagonal tail difference can be summed exactly. The approximation below leaves only a squared-Mersenne tail to estimate.

Proposition 6.128 (An exact rational approximation formula). For integers H,D≥0H,D\ge0, with the integer prefixes ΦN\Phi_N defined above, R2H−RH−[ΦH−Φ2H+2H(2H−1)(12+∑d=1Dμ(d)(2d−1)2)]=2H(2H−1)∑d>Dμ(d)(2d−1)2.\begin{aligned} R_{2H}-R_H &-\left[\Phi_H-\Phi_{2H} +2^H(2^H-1)\left(\frac12+\sum_{d=1}^{D}\frac{\mu(d)}{(2^d-1)^2}\right)\right]\\ &=2^H(2^H-1)\sum_{d>D}\frac{\mu(d)}{(2^d-1)^2}. \end{aligned} This follows by substituting the squared-denominator identity for SS into R2H−RH=2H(2H−1)S+ΦH−Φ2HR_{2H}-R_H=2^H(2^H-1)S+\Phi_H-\Phi_{2H}. There is no required ordering between DD and HH. .

Divisor terms and their complement

At H=6H=6 and s=2s=2, the difference φ(2H+s)−φ(H+s)=φ(14)−φ(8)\varphi(2H+s)-\varphi(H+s)=\varphi(14)-\varphi(8) is 22, whereas the terms with divisor index d∣Hd\mid H sum to 33. The other indices contribute −1-1. The following decomposition keeps both contributions. It holds for every positive integer HH, not only a least common multiple; an estimate is needed before its second sum can be discarded.

Proposition 6.131 (The sum over divisor indices). For integers H>0H>0 and s≥0s\ge0, the part of the Möbius expansion indexed by divisors of HH is ∑d∣Hd∣sμ(d)Hd=Hφ(gcd⁡(H,s))gcd⁡(H,s).\sum_{\substack{d\mid H\\d\mid s}}\mu(d)\frac Hd =H\frac{\varphi(\gcd(H,s))}{\gcd(H,s)}. The formal statement writes the same value after extracting H/rad⁡(H)H/\operatorname{rad}(H), where rad⁡(H)=∏p∣Hp\operatorname{rad}(H)=\prod_{p\mid H}p. .

A numerator polynomial with explicit positive coefficients

Multiples of a period

Allowing positive multiples of a prescribed period gives another criterion equivalent to irrationality of SS. Sufficiency follows by telescoping the tail-period identity, and necessity follows from completeness of the residue test. The equivalence is proved, but its quantified arithmetic condition is not established. The finite examples below give denominator exclusions whose overlap with the diagonal certificates is described explicitly.

Theorem 6.159 (Concatenation and specified period multiples). For nonnegative integers a,b,Na,b,N, define the integer block sum Qa,N=∑j=1aφ(N+j)2a−j.Q_{a,N}=\sum_{j=1}^{a}\varphi(N+j)2^{a-j}. Splitting a block after its first aa terms gives Qa+b,N=2bQa,N+Qb,N+a.Q_{a+b,N}=2^bQ_{a,N}+Q_{b,N+a}. In particular, Q2h,N=2hQh,N+Qh,N+hQ_{2h,N}=2^hQ_{h,N}+Q_{h,N+h}. The corresponding cyclotomic identity is Φ4(2h)=22h+1=Φ2(22h)\Phi_4(2^h)=2^{2h}+1=\Phi_2(2^{2h}): the order-four factor at height hh is the order-two factor at height 2h2h.

The order-three factor is different: Φ3(2h)=22h+2h+1\Phi_3(2^h)=2^{2h}+2^h+1 comes from tripling the period. It is not generally part of the doubling sequence. For example, Φ3(2)=7\Phi_3(2)=7 divides none of 22j−12^{2^j}-1, because the order of 22 modulo 77 is 33, which does not divide 2j2^j. Thus the block identities relate specified period multiples; they do not put all the order-two, order-three and order-four factors into one doubling chain. .

The strict prime-position criterion

A sufficient prime-index condition is that, for every integer h≥1h\ge1 and every N0≥0N_0\ge0, there is a prime p≥max⁡(N0+h+1,h+5)p\ge\max(N_0+h+1,h+5) such that Re⁡e(2p−h−1(2h−1)S)<910.\operatorname{Re}e\bigl(2^{p-h-1}(2^h-1)S\bigr)<\frac9{10}. Here e(x)=exp⁡(2πix)e(x)=\exp(2\pi i x). The positive difference between 9/109/10 and this real part may depend on the chosen prime; the truncation depth is then chosen so that its error fits within that difference. This is a weaker phase requirement than the earlier bound 4/54/5, not a larger saving from 11. The implication to irrationality is proved, but the displayed prime-index condition remains unproved. (implication proved; antecedent [Open]) .

Finite Euler-product identities

These are identities for the Dirichlet-convolution square μ*μ\mu*\mu, not the pointwise square μ(n)2\mu(n)^2. For each prime pp, its coefficients at 1,p,p21,p,p^2 are 1,−2,11,-2,1, and the higher prime-power coefficients vanish. The local factors at exponents 11 and 22 are 1−2p+1p2=(1−1p)2,1−2p2+1p4=(1−1p2)2.1-\frac2p+\frac1{p^2}=\left(1-\frac1p\right)^2, \qquad 1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac1{p^4}=\left(1-\frac1{p^2}\right)^2. For a prime pp and e≥0e\ge0, the corresponding convolution with the divisor-sum function σ\sigma gives σ(pe+2)−2σ(pe+1)+σ(pe)=pe+1(p−1)=φ(pe+2).\sigma(p^{e+2})-2\sigma(p^{e+1})+\sigma(p^e) =p^{e+1}(p-1)=\varphi(p^{e+2}). This follows by subtracting the finite geometric sums. These finite identities do not assert a transcendence result. .

Parameter ranges and quantifiers

The table records parameter ranges and quantifiers. “Fixed” refers to listed examples, “bounded” to a finite range, and “cofinal” to a statement of the form ∀N0∃N≥N0\forall N_0\,\exists N\ge N_0. A bound of the form ∀a≥8\forall a\ge8 is not finite-range evidence: it gives a conclusion at all sufficiently large parameters. “Uniform” describes the quantification of a statement, not whether all hypotheses needed to apply it are proved. A bound on a secondary variable, such as j<2⋅2aj<2\cdot2^a, does not restrict the scale aa to a finite range. Such parameter-uniform results are grouped with the uniform statements, not with finite calculations.

Some identities have no distinguished scale parameter. They are listed with the general identities. An equivalence can hold for all parameters without establishing either of the equivalent arithmetic assertions.

The LCM formulation of Problem 249 requires arbitrarily large scales: Irrational(∑n≥1φ(n)/2n)⇔∀a0∃a≥a0,Ωa∉ℤ,\mathrm{Irrational}\Bigl(\sum_{n\ge 1}\varphi(n)/2^n\Bigr) \iff \forall a_0\ \exists a\ge a_0,\ \Omega_a \notin \mathbb Z, a cofinal statement in the exponent aa indexing H=H(2a)H=H(2^a). A finite calculation alone does not establish it; a further theorem could propagate finite information to arbitrarily large scales.

The table groups statements by their parameter ranges, not by proof status. In particular, some assertions with cofinal quantifiers are already proved, such as the prime constructions and rational comparison sequences. Others are implications whose quantified hypotheses remain open. The horizontal rule separates the cofinal group for ease of reference; it does not mark a boundary between proved and unproved mathematics. The descriptions identify this distinction in that group. The prefixes summarise the quantifiers; complete hypotheses are given in the cited statements. A definition records an object or condition; it does not by itself prove the associated soundness or existence assertion.

In the periodic-weight rows, write w:ℕ→ℤw:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z and cw(n)=∑d∣nw(d)c_w(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}w(d) for n≥1n\ge1. Positivity and nonvanishing refer to these divisor coefficients, not to the weight ww itself. Here “nonzero arbitrarily far out” means that for every NN there is n>Nn>N with cw(n)≠0c_w(n)\ne0; it does not mean nonvanishing on every arithmetic progression. The nonprincipal character χ4\chi_4 modulo four is 00 on even integers and (−1)(n−1)/2(-1)^{(n-1)/2} on odd integers.

What extending a finite calculation would require

A finite computation can be extended by further computation or by a uniform argument. The following examples distinguish these possibilities from parameter-uniform theorems that are already proved. They do not assert that a computational bound is intrinsic to a method.

  1. Finite certificate tables. Results such as (28 explicit values of tt through t=64t{=}64, now a strict subset of the aggregate ∀t≤82\forall t\le82 band), (h∈[1,8]h\in[1,8] at fixed depth 16), and (h∈[1,16]h\in[1,16] at exponent 14) are each a finite list of independently verified rows, not a single argument instantiated at a free parameter. The existing lists do not establish further rows; an extension needs either additional computations or an argument for a family of parameters.

  2. A bounded window inside a uniform theorem. The results and hold for every a≥8a\ge8, subject to their stated bounds on the other parameters. In the sign theorem, for example, J+a+6<2⋅2aJ+a+6<2\cdot2^a. Their proofs are therefore not merely enumerations of a fixed set of exponents. The missing conclusion is a suitable residue inequality at arbitrarily large scales, not extension of the range of aa in the positivity theorem. No complexity lower bound follows from this audit.

  3. Parameter dependence in an approximation estimate. For reduced approximants pK/qKp_K/q_K to SS, the conditions 0<|S−pK/qK|≤εK0<|S-p_K/q_K|\le\varepsilon_K and qKεK→0q_K\varepsilon_K\to0 imply irrationality. A growing denominator alone does not control this product. In particular, the exact reduced-denominator formula concerns a specified finite Möbius sum; it does not estimate the complementary tail. Likewise, a bound proved with a constant depending on a fixed auxiliary parameter is not automatically uniform when that parameter grows. Both the dependence of the constant and the error estimate must be retained in any passage to an unbounded family.

The missing arithmetic inputs include the stated constant-saving exponential-sum estimate and an upper-endpoint residue inequality. For the positivity theorem, the unresolved step is exclusion of that residue interval, not positivity at more exponents.

Relations between the representations

The formulas below express the same series through binary tails, Möbius sums, rational approximations and exponential sums. Each identity permits a change of variables or representation. A limitation of one proposed argument does not automatically apply after that change: its hypotheses must be checked for the new objects. The last subsection illustrates this distinction with finite-state decoding and polynomial denominator identities.

Binary tails and Möbius sums

Erdős’s argument for ∑n1/(2n−1)\sum_n1/(2^n-1) chooses congruences so that divisor counts along a block are divisible by increasing powers of the base. A tail bound then forces a long run of zero digits [9]. It uses no finite automaton.

A different proposal would recover each later block from a fixed finite summary of the preceding history. The balanced-pulse counterexample shows why that proposal fails for the family constructed there. For m≥2m\ge2, its members have the same earlier history but different successors. A state that identifies all those histories cannot recover every successor. More generally, an exact label-and-decoder pair for that family needs at least ⌊(m+1)/2⌋+1\lfloor(m+1)/2\rfloor+1 distinct labels. This is a lower bound on the number of labels, not a linear lower bound on the number of bits, and it is not a state-complexity theorem for the actual totient sequence. [Lean] [uniform] .

The cofinal certificate implication is a separate theorem. The counterexample above neither proves its hypothesis nor makes it the only possible route to irrationality. Likewise, shows that inverse-phase column weights can preserve a determinant, and gives the exact growing ranks of totient sections. These are different statements with different hypotheses; none is a general prohibition on other representations of SS.

The Möbius representation instead allows the identity to be applied to μ\mu, since |μ(d)|≤d|\mu(d)|\le d for d≥1d\ge1. The polynomial identities from to operate at each finite radical without an autonomous decoder. The exact reduced denominator and its lower bound are then given by and . Those formulas concern a finite rational contribution. They do not exclude cancellation by the complementary tail and hence do not settle irrationality. The representations are equal expressions for SS; what differs is the information supplied by the particular arguments.

Index of unproved conditions

This section collects the unproved hypotheses used by the conditional results above. For each one, it states the additional arithmetic assertion and the implication to S∉ℚS\notin\mathbb Q. A proof of an implication is not a proof of its hypothesis. The record does not settle whether S=∑n≥0φ(n)2−nS=\sum_{n\ge0}\varphi(n)2^{-n} is irrational.

How to use the index

Each entry separates the proved implication from the additional hypothesis needed to apply it. The comparison concerns the displayed statements, not the prospects of an entire method.

The range tags describe quantification, not a ranking of mathematical strength. [fixed] records finitely many explicit instances; [bounded] records the displayed bounded parameter range; [uniform] ranges over every allowed value of the stated parameters; and [cofinal] includes a quantifier of the form ∀a0∃a≥a0\forall a_0\ \exists a\ge a_0. All other hypotheses and quantifiers remain part of the statement. A cofinal assertion about a different quantity, or with a different order of quantifiers, need not supply the irrationality condition. [n/a] denotes the absence of a relevant growing parameter. Proof status is recorded separately by [Lean], [Cert], [Math], [Cited] and [Open], as in the reading guide; a uniform or cofinal statement may itself be proved or may remain an unproved hypothesis.

It starts with the exponential-sum estimate, then gives thirteen further approaches with their individual hypotheses and source references.
