What the preceding comparisons show

The comparison separates three issues. A block estimate with a fixed saving in the real part or norm of an exponential sum would provide certificates. The upper-endpoint conditions instead ask for a particular residue or size estimate along an LCM sequence. Their sufficient forms are related by Proposition 9.14, but those implications do not prove any of the arithmetic hypotheses.

The generic bounded-rank argument fails for a separate reason: the rational comparison sequence has unbounded section rank. A totient-specific upper bound would require hypotheses not shared by that sequence.

These are statements about the displayed conditions and comparisons, not an exhaustive classification of possible proofs. Some conditions are equivalent to irrationality; others are only sufficient. No relative difficulty, truth probability, or independent formal verification follows from their position in the table.

Counterexamples to proposed deductions

The following examples disprove particular deductions proposed for S=∑n≥1φ(n)2−nS=\sum_{n\ge1}\varphi(n)2^{-n}. Each example specifies the assumptions that it satisfies and the conclusion that fails. Some concern other coefficient sequences; others concern a particular way of estimating a totient sum. Neither kind decides the irrationality of SS, and neither excludes arguments using additional properties of φ\varphi.

Changing the coefficients after a finite prefix

(a) Proposed argument. The quantified residue condition requires certificates beyond every starting index. A finite computation can check many instances, but one fixed inspection bound cannot establish these quantifiers. The following comparison explains this limitation without making any claim about all possible irrationality arguments.

(b) Counterexample. Theorem 2.4 gives an explicit splice construction; its series value, exact reduced denominator and failure of the separation condition are checked in Lean ([Lean]). Choose an integer P>BP>B, set γ(n)=φ(n)\gamma(n)=\varphi(n) for n≤Bn\le B, and γ(n)=n−𝟏P∣n\gamma(n)=n-\mathbf 1_{P\mid n} for n>Bn>B. Then 0≤γ(n)≤n0\le\gamma(n)\le n, and the binary series ∑γ(n)/2n\sum\gamma(n)/2^n is rational: it is a finite rational prefix, plus the tail of ∑nn2−n\sum_n n2^{-n}, minus a geometric sum over the multiples of PP beyond BB. Because γ\gamma agrees with φ\varphi on every index ≤B\le B, γ\gamma passes every finite certificate that only inspects indices ≤B\le B; in particular it passes or fails every instance of 𝒞(h,N,L)\mathcal{C}(h,N,L) with N+h+L≤BN+h+L\le B exactly as φ\varphi does. Yet ∑γ(n)/2n∈ℚ\sum\gamma(n)/2^n\in\mathbb Q by construction.

(c) Scope. For each fixed bound BB, a different rational comparison sequence can agree with φ\varphi on all inspected coefficients. This rules out a deduction from that finite prefix alone. It does not rule out a proof that establishes the required instances for arbitrarily large BB with the correct quantifiers. Such a proof would no longer be a single finite inspection. The comparison also does not preserve multiplicativity or every other arithmetic property of φ\varphi.

(d) Consequence. The finite-prefix example and the parity example below are distinct constructions. The former preserves a prescribed finite prefix; the latter preserves parity and has separated nonperiodic blocks. Each shows why its own list of assumptions is insufficient. The recorded finite diagonal examples remain useful individual certificates, but their number alone gives no assertion at arbitrarily large scales.

A rational series with matching totient parity

(a) Proposed argument. Consider the claim that a uniformly bounded sequence c:ℕ→ℕc:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}, with c(n)≤nc(n)\le n, exact totient parity and no eventual period, must have an irrational binary sum. The next example refutes this claim. It also has arbitrarily many paired changes beyond every threshold, with an arbitrarily prescribed minimum separation.

(b) Construction. Start with the sequence 0,1,1,2,4,4,4,…0,1,1,2,4,4,4,\ldots. At each position m=2k+3m=2^{k+3}, k≥0k\ge0, replace the pair (4,4)(4,4) at m,m+1m,m+1 by (6,0)(6,0). Equivalently, c(n)={0,n=0,1,n=1,2,2,n=3,6,n=2k+3 for some k≥0,0,n=2k+3+1 for some k≥0,4,otherwise.c(n)= \begin{cases} 0,&n=0,\\ 1,&n=1,2,\\ 2,&n=3,\\ 6,&n=2^{k+3}\text{ for some }k\ge0,\\ 0,&n=2^{k+3}+1\text{ for some }k\ge0,\\ 4,&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases} Each replacement leaves the binary sum unchanged because 2⋅2−m−4⋅2−(m+1)=02\cdot2^{-m}-4\cdot2^{-(m+1)}=0. The increasingly large gaps between replacements prevent eventual periodicity. The strongest recorded result also quantifies their separation:

Proposition 10.1 (A rational series preserving totient parity and the stated separation properties). There exists c:ℕ→ℕc:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N such that: c(n)≤6c(n)\le6 for all nn; c(n)≤nc(n)\le n; c(n)≡φ(n)(mod⁡2)c(n)\equiv\varphi(n)\pmod2 for every nn; for every N,G,KN,G,K there is a block of KK explicit (6,0)(6,0) carry-pulse pairs beyond NN, each pair separated by more than GG; and ∑nc(n)/2n=3/2\sum_n c(n)/2^n = 3/2.

(sum computation ; non-periodicity ; exact parity match ). [Lean] [cofinal] .

(c) Scope. The displayed bounds, parity agreement and aperiodicity, including the stated number and separation of the edits, are jointly compatible with a rational binary sum. They therefore do not imply irrationality. The sequence cc differs from φ\varphi: the example preserves its parity, not all its arithmetic properties. It excludes an argument using only the listed assumptions, not every strengthening of an aperiodicity condition or every use of totient coefficients.

(d) Consequence. The paired edits have zero total contribution, since 2⋅2−m−4⋅2−(m+1)=02\cdot2^{-m}-4\cdot2^{-(m+1)}=0. Applied at the specified sparse positions of this particular base sequence, they preserve the rational sum and the required bounds while preventing eventual periodicity. This does not construct a rational series for every prescribed parity pattern, and it is not the finite-prefix construction of Theorem 2.4. A proposed criterion using only the assumptions of this example must fail; a criterion using further arithmetic information is not addressed.

What the square-CRT construction proves

For a prime pp and m≥1m\ge1, φ(pm)=(p−1)φ(m)+𝟏p∣mφ(m).\varphi(pm)=(p-1)\varphi(m)+\mathbf1_{p\mid m}\varphi(m). A congruence modulo p2p^2 can prescribe the cofactor modulo pp and hence remove the second term over a chosen finite range. This makes each product formula simpler; it does not imply that differences of the resulting values are nonzero.

The examples in Observation 6.117 show both possibilities. At n=52n=52, the offset pairs (13,13)(13,13) and (26,18)(26,18) give respectively φ(65)−φ(65)=0\varphi(65)-\varphi(65)=0 and φ(78)−φ(70)=0\varphi(78)-\varphi(70)=0 (). All four prime–cofactor products are coprime (). At n=27n=27, the offset pairs (3,3)(3,3) and (6,8)(6,8) instead give φ(30)−φ(30)=0\varphi(30)-\varphi(30)=0 and φ(33)−φ(35)=−4\varphi(33)-\varphi(35)=-4 (), again with coprime factors (). These finite equalities are checked by exact arithmetic. No minimality claim about either witness is needed. The general existence theorem supplies a common base for the stated finite congruence requirements, not a nonvanishing assertion. [Cert] [fixed] .

The vanishing example disproves the implication from correction-free factorisation to nonvanishing; the other example shows that this factorisation does not force vanishing either. This does not establish formal independence of two propositions, or exclude an argument using additional hypotheses. The prime-dilation identity and the CRT constructions , remain available with their own prime and residue hypotheses.

A separate elementary identity in the same file concerns alternating sums. Let II be finite, let i∉Ii\notin I, and suppose an integer-valued function ff on finite subsets satisfies f(T∪{i})=f(T)f(T\cup\{i\})=f(T) for every T⊆IT\subseteq I. Pairing TT with T∪{i}T\cup\{i\} gives ∑T⊆I∪{i}(−1)|T|f(T)=0.\sum_{T\subseteq I\cup\{i\}}(-1)^{|T|}f(T)=0. This is the content of . It has no totient hypothesis, but an application must still verify invariance under the indicated insertion. Neither it nor the congruence construction supplies the missing nonzero totient difference at a prescribed LCM height.

The cost of clearing a rational denominator

For example, multiplying 5/125/12 by 44 gives 5/35/3: the factor 44 removed from the denominator appears in the multiplier. The following lemma gives the exact divisibility behind this calculation. It concerns ordinary reduced fractions, without assumptions on totients.

Lemma 10.2 (Complement divisibility after multiplication). Write x=a/bx=a/b in lowest terms, where a∈ℤa\in\mathbb{Z} and b≥1b\ge1. Let c∈ℤc\in\mathbb{Z} and let HH be a positive divisor of bb. If the reduced denominator of cxcx divides HH, then b/H∣c.b/H\mid c.

. Indeed, the hypothesis makes Hcx=Hca/bHcx=Hca/b integral. Since gcd⁡(a,b)=1\gcd(a,b)=1, it follows that b∣Hcb\mid Hc, hence b/H∣cb/H\mid c. Writing c=(b/H)tc=(b/H)t also gives Hcx=taHcx=ta; this equality is recorded in . If c≠0c\ne0, the divisibility implies |c|≥b/H|c|\ge b/H. The nonzero hypothesis is essential for this size bound: c=0c=0 has reduced denominator one and satisfies the divisibility, but has no positive size cost. The lemma is about multiplication of one rational value, not arbitrary cancellations among several values.

A related elementary inequality compares a positive numerator with its denominator. If a>0a>0, r≥0r\ge0, n≥1n\ge1, 2r∣a2^r\mid a, and a/b<2/(2n−1)a/b<2/(2^n-1), then 2r(2n−1)≤a(2n−1)<2b.2^r(2^n-1)\le a(2^n-1)<2b. The source gives this Mersenne instance and the version with general positive denominator parameter . Positivity of aa is what turns numerator divisibility into a lower bound; it cannot be omitted.

The accompanying linear-algebra statement has a one-dimensional quotient. Let V,WV,W be vector spaces over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, let ev:V→ℚ\mathrm{ev}:V\to\mathbb{Q} and Λ:V→W\Lambda:V\to W be linear, and suppose ker⁡ev⊆ker⁡Λ\ker\mathrm{ev}\subseteq\ker\Lambda. Choose e∈Ve\in V with ev(e)=1\mathrm{ev}(e)=1. Then, for every v∈Vv\in V, v−ev(v)e∈ker⁡ev,Λ(v)=ev(v)Λ(e).v-\mathrm{ev}(v)e\in\ker\mathrm{ev},\qquad \Lambda(v)=\mathrm{ev}(v)\Lambda(e). This is factorisation through the scalar quotient V/ker⁡evV/\ker\mathrm{ev} (). A surjection onto a higher-dimensional space would imply only a linear factorisation through that space, not multiplication by one fixed vector.

The denominator calculations use and . For integers aa and D≥1D\ge1, the reduced denominator of a/Da/D is D/gcd⁡(|a|,D)D/\gcd(|a|,D). Hence a divisor of DD coprime to aa divides the reduced denominator. Coprimality is sufficient, not necessary: 2/8=1/42/8=1/4 retains the divisor 22. More generally, if CC is a positive divisor of DD, gcd⁡(C,a)=1\gcd(C,a)=1, and h≥0h\ge0 is an integer, then C/gcd⁡(C,h)C/\gcd(C,h) divides the reduced denominator of ha/Dha/D. At h=0h=0 this assertion retains only the divisor one. [Lean] [uniform] .

For a nonzero multiplier, a lower bound for b/Hb/H therefore gives a lower bound for its absolute value. Signed moments and parity

A determinant construction needs a nonzero numerator as well as a small approximation error. The following parity test can establish the first requirement for a specified finite sum.

Lemma 10.3 (Nonvanishing from a unique largest denominator exponent). Let II be a finite set, let ui∈ℤu_i\in\mathbb{Z} and ei∈ℕe_i\in\mathbb{N} for i∈Ii\in I, and suppose that m∈Im\in I satisfies ei<eme_i<e_m for every i≠mi\ne m. If umu_m is odd, then 2em∑i∈Iui2ei=∑i∈Iui2em−ei≡1(mod⁡2).2^{e_m}\sum_{i\in I}\frac{u_i}{2^{e_i}} =\sum_{i\in I}u_i2^{e_m-e_i}\equiv1\pmod2. In particular, the sum is nonzero.

Lean: signed_dyadic_clearing, signed_dyadic_sum_ne_zero, scaled_dyadic_sum_odd.

Every term except umu_m is even, which proves the assertion. For example, 1/2−1/8=3/81/2-1/8=3/8 has odd cleared numerator. Uniqueness is necessary for this argument: two odd contributions with the same largest exponent can cancel. The formal statement is .

The same file gives a separate determinant expansion from the Leibniz formula , together with the truncated signed moments ∑N=1YaN2−N(k+1)\sum_{N=1}^Y a_N2^{-N(k+1)} and their Hankel determinants ( and ). The parity lemma is not derived from that determinant identity. A determinant application must first identify a sum to which the parity hypotheses apply. [Lean] [uniform] .

For the totient series, one would still need suitable configurations at arbitrarily large scales and a denominator-weighted error tending to zero. Nonvanishing alone provides neither. No such family is supplied by these two algebraic statements; compare the separate rank discussion in §10.8. In another base, the analogous argument would require divisibility by a prime factor of that base rather than an unchanged appeal to parity.

Column rescaling does not certify cancellation

A nonzero determinant need not prevent one row from being constant. For example, (111−1)(100−1)=(1−111).\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}. The first and last matrices have determinants −2-2 and 22, respectively; the second row of the resulting matrix is constant. This simple column rescaling matters when a determinant is proposed as evidence for cancellation in the first-harmonic sums ().

Proposition 10.4 (A nonzero minor survives inverse-phase column weights). Let d≥1d\ge1 be an integer, let e0,…,ed−1e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1} be nonnegative integers, and let z0,…,zd−1z_0,\ldots,z_{d-1} be nonzero complex numbers. Write Pij=zjeiP_{ij}=z_j^{e_i}, and suppose ei0=1e_{i_0}=1 for some i0i_0. Multiplying column jj by Wj=zj−1W_j=z_j^{-1} gives (Pdiag⁡(W))i0j=1,det⁡(Pdiag⁡(W))=det⁡(P)∏j=0d−1zj−1.(P\operatorname{diag}(W))_{i_0j}=1,\qquad \det(P\operatorname{diag}(W))=\det(P)\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}z_j^{-1}. Thus a nonzero determinant remains nonzero while row i0i_0 becomes constant. If all |zj|=1|z_j|=1, its absolute value is also unchanged.

The entry formula and the determinant of a product prove the statement (, ). If row-dependent weights are allowed, the choice Wij=zji/zjeiW_{ij}=z_j^i/z_j^{e_i} gives WijPij=zjiW_{ij}P_{ij}=z_j^i and makes row zero constant. It produces the ordinary Vandermonde matrix, which is nonsingular when the zjz_j are pairwise distinct (, ). [Lean] [uniform] .

These are statements about complex matrices, not arithmetic properties of the totient sequence. In particular, determinant nonvanishing, even with unit-modulus weights, does not by itself exclude complete alignment in the indicated row. An application of the first-harmonic criterion () needs additional information that excludes such weights or controls the resulting weighted sum. The example does not require that information to take the form of an identity coupling different rows, and it does not rule out determinant arguments that use appropriate additional hypotheses.

(c) Scope. Eventual integrality on the LCM grid is a necessary consequence of rationality, not a claim about the actual series made without that hypothesis. The finite-grid test uses the individual one-sided bounds Bq<2LB_q<2^L, rather than charging the larger radius to both ends of a pairwise interval. This compares modulus bounds, not binary depths. A finite nonempty set and every stated size inequality are needed; three or more points and pairwise compatibility are not.

Neither statement supplies the unbounded family required to decide #249. Exhibiting a nonintegral tail difference on the LCM grid at arbitrarily large tt would refute rationality. The finite-grid test is a way to certify such a difference, not a proof that these tests succeed at arbitrarily large scales.

The implication from rationality to grid flatness () should not be confused with an assertion of flatness for the actual series. The exact diagonal integrality reformulation and its quantified converse (, ) give other equivalent forms of the problem. They are not the only such forms; Proposition 1.8 lists further equivalent certificate conditions.

(d) Consequence. Choosing the least deep tail is the step that turns a common-fractional-part assumption into an intersection of arcs. A related finite comparison concerns first and second differences: at (h,N)=(1,8)(h,N)=(1,8) the first-difference test holds at depth 88, while no second-difference certificate exists at depth at most 88 (). This disproves a universal claim of smaller depth for second differences; it does not show that they can never improve a certificate.

Exact dyadic rank and the limits of a rank argument

(a) The question. Which linear relations hold among the sections n↦φ(2jn+r)n\mapsto\varphi(2^j n+r), and how does their span grow as the level increases? Coons had already proved nonregularity in every base k≥2k\ge2  [Cited]. The result below identifies a basis and gives the exact rank at each dyadic level. Martin’s Theorem 1 implies the independence of the positive-residue affine forms ; the two sections with residue zero need a separate argument. The short note gives the all-base proof and the integral relations.

(b) Construction.

Theorem 10.7 (Exact dyadic rank and infinite-dimensionality). For every e≥1e\ge1, the family {n↦φ(n),n↦φ(2n)}∪{n↦φ(2jn+r):1≤j≤e,0<r<2j,r odd}\{n\mapsto\varphi(n),\ n\mapsto\varphi(2n)\} \ \cup\ \{n\mapsto\varphi(2^j n+r):1\le j\le e,\ 0<r<2^j,\ r\text{ odd}\} is linearly independent over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. It contains 2e+12^e+1 sequences () and spans the sections through level ee by the zero- and even-residue reductions.

The forms nn and 2n2n are proportional, so their coefficients need a separate argument. Restrict a proposed relation to n=2m+1n=2m+1, where φ(2n)=φ(n)\varphi(2n)=\varphi(n). The odd-residue sections and φ(n)\varphi(n) then correspond to pairwise nonproportional forms. CRT and Dirichlet’s theorem separate them by an evaluation matrix: make the primitive part of one form prime and force suitable prime divisors into the others. This kills the positive-residue coefficients and gives A+B=0A+B=0 for the two remaining coefficients. Evaluating their relation at n=2n=2 gives A+2B=0A+2B=0. Hence both vanish. This gives the dyadic specialization of the proof in the short note. The formal independence statement is ; consequently the full infinite family spans an infinite-dimensional ℚ\mathbb Q-space, . There are no Q,v∈ℕ>0Q,v\in\mathbb{N}_{>0} and A,b∈ℤA,b\in\mathbb{Z} with QvA=bQvA=b, A≠0A\ne0, and |b|<Qv|b|<Qv: the identity forces |b|=Qv|A|≥Qv|b|=Qv|A|\ge Qv. [Lean] [uniform] (holds for every e≥1e\ge1; existence side is unconditional, via Mathlib’s CRT + primes-in-AP machinery) (dyadic totient-kernel; not the Möbius coordinate).

The Lean independence theorem is also stated for e=0e=0, but its auxiliary canonical index then still contains the two zero-residue sections φ(n)\varphi(n) and φ(2n)\varphi(2n). It is therefore not the actual truncation through level zero, which consists only of φ(n)\varphi(n) and has dimension one.

Integral relations.

The independence statement also determines the arithmetic of the section lattice. Fix e≥1e\ge1, write Fj,r(n)=φ(2jn+r)F_{j,r}(n)=\varphi(2^j n+r), and let Ie={(j,r):0≤j≤e,0≤r<2j}I_e=\{(j,r):0\le j\le e,\ 0\le r<2^j\}. Retain F0,0F_{0,0}, F1,0F_{1,0}, and the odd-residue sections at levels 1,…,e1,\ldots,e; call this retained index set JeJ_e. The totient identities reduce every omitted section to Fi=aiFj(i)F_i=a_iF_{j(i)} for a retained section j(i)j(i) and an integer ai≥0a_i\ge0. Thus the retained family generates the lattice Le=∑i∈IeℤFiL_e=\sum_{i\in I_e}\mathbb Z F_i. Its rational independence gives integer independence as well: every element of LeL_e has unique integer coordinates in these 2e+12^e+1 retained sections.

To describe all integral relations, let EiE_i denote the formal coordinate vector in ℤIe\mathbb Z^{I_e} and use the evaluation map $$\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{$\displaystyle \operatorname{ev}_e:\mathbb Z^{I_e}\longrightarrow L_e, \qquad (c_i)\longmapsto\sum_{i\in I_e}c_iF_i. $}$$ For each omitted index put Ri=Ei−aiEj(i)R_i=E_i-a_iE_{j(i)}. Then $$\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{$\displaystyle \ker(\operatorname{ev}_e) =\bigoplus_{i\in I_e\mathbin{\backslash} J_e}\mathbb Z R_i, \qquad \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Z}\ker(\operatorname{ev}_e)=2^e-2. $}$$ Indeed, subtracting ∑i∉JeciRi\sum_{i\notin J_e}c_iR_i from a relation removes all omitted coordinates. The remainder is a relation among retained sections, so independence makes it zero. Conversely, the coefficient of EiE_i in ∑h∉JebhRh\sum_{h\notin J_e}b_hR_h is exactly bib_i, proving uniqueness. The decisive feature is the unit pivot 11 in each omitted coordinate (or −1-1 if a relation is oriented oppositely). Elimination uses no division; it therefore identifies the integral relation lattice, not merely its rational span. The depth-two example in the short note illustrates these two-term rows. The distinction between the retained basis and the redundant spanning family of all sections already matters for kk-regular sequences that are not eventually zero: their growth exponent is the base-kk logarithm of the joint spectral radius of their section matrices in a basis, whereas a redundant spanning family gives only an upper bound (Coons [3]) [Cited]. The totient is not regular, so that theorem does not apply; the short note records how the section maps act on the retained bases from one level to the next.

The integral normal form and the full dyadic rational basis are formally checked in Lean. The formal statement gives the same construction for every integer base k≥2k\ge2, with relation rank ∑j=1e−1kj\sum_{j=1}^{e-1}k^j. The full dyadic assembly separately gives a basis for the infinite rational span and for its finitely supported rational relations. These finite and infinite statements should not be confused with a claim about infinite sums of relations.

(c) What the rank theorem does not prove. Infinite section rank does not imply irrationality of SS. The result quantifies the nonregularity already cited above: it gives the rank, the retained sections and their integral relations. Martin’s simultaneous inequalities supply another proof for pairwise nonproportional affine forms with positive slopes [4] [Cited]. His theorem does not separate nn from 2n2n; the two evaluations above do that. The linked Lean proof is independent of Martin’s theorem.

Indeed, for each odd rr with 0<r<2j0<r<2^j, the recurrence gives vφ(2jn+r)=2u2jn+r−1−u2jn+r.v\varphi(2^j n+r)=2u_{2^j n+r-1}-u_{2^j n+r}. These 2e−12^e-1 totient sections are independent and belong to the span of the displayed carry sections after multiplication by v≠0v\ne0. The rank bound follows. The boundary condition uN/2N→0u_N/2^N\to0 identifies the canonical carry, but is not used in this rank-transfer argument.

To contradict rationality by rank, one would also need an incompatible upper bound. The comparison series with value 5/45/4 in Section 12.6 shows why rationality, a binary carry recurrence and linear coefficient growth alone do not supply such a bound. Its coefficients agree with φ\varphi at odd indices but differ at even indices; they are not the totient sequence. Thus this comparison does not exclude an argument using additional totient identities.

A separate finite-dimensional calculation concerns the matrix UN(i,j)=μ((i+1)/(j+1))U_N(i,j)=\mu((i+1)/(j+1)) when (j+1)∣(i+1)(j+1)\mid(i+1) and zero otherwise, for 0≤i,j<N0\le i,j<N. It is lower triangular with diagonal entries one. Hence det⁡UN=1\det U_N=1 and the map x↦UNxx\mapsto U_Nx is injective (). This proves injectivity of that particular map, not the impossibility of every finite-dimensional argument for irrationality.

(d) The evaluation-matrix argument. For functions f1,…,fsf_1,\ldots,f_s with values in a field, points n1,…,nsn_1,\ldots,n_s for which det⁡(fj(ni))≠0\det(f_j(n_i))\ne0 prove linear independence: evaluating a relation gives an invertible linear system for its coefficients. This elementary criterion is the content of and . It does not, by itself, construct the points. Here the totient formula, CRT and Dirichlet’s theorem provide them for nonproportional affine forms, followed by the separate zero-residue argument. Another arithmetic function would require its own argument for nonvanishing of the evaluation determinant.

Why the stated hypotheses cannot be omitted

A conditional theorem can hold at every scale while its arithmetic hypothesis is known at only a few scales, or at none. The distinctions below concern the specific implications already stated. They are not claims that every argument using the same objects must fail.

Implications concerning the totient series

Cancellation versus a certificate.

The first-harmonic implication converts the stated cosine bound on one block into a finite residue certificate (). To prove irrationality, the bound must hold with the quantifiers in Section 3: for every shift and beyond every block threshold. A finite identity for the sum, or a computation at one block, does not establish this assertion.

Sign versus distance from an integer.

The positivity theorem for the LCM tail difference () identifies the relevant endpoint under the stated room and modulus bounds. Nonintegrality follows only after excluding the corresponding residue interval (). Likewise, the terminal-dominance condition is a sufficient hypothesis, not a construction of the required parameters (). Under integrality its inequality contradicts positivity of the terminal carry; the contradiction establishes sufficiency, not the inequality itself.

An error bound versus a separated approximation.

The finite-tail approximation has a uniform error radius (). The cited exact check supplies nonintegrality at the two exponents a=4,6a=4,6 (); it is not an assertion that no other exponent works. To obtain irrationality by this criterion, separation must occur at arbitrarily large LCM scales. In the nondivisor approximation of Section 6.6.8, the error bound is also proved when D≥2HD\ge2H. Its remaining requirement is finite rational separation, not an additional convergence hypothesis.

Denominator growth versus approximation quality.

The lower bound for the product of the upper-half Mersenne factors () concerns a denominator expression. An irrationality argument needs a comparison with the error of the corresponding approximation. Growth of that denominator expression alone does not give either a successful residue test or a nonintegral totient tail.

A rank lower bound versus a contradiction.

The coefficient independence and hypothetical-carry rank bounds hold uniformly in the level (, ). A contradiction would require an upper bound for the actual carry that is strictly smaller than the lower bound at some level. The rational 5/45/4 comparison disproves the proposed generic upper bound. The separate integer boundary conditions in the cited adjugate calculation are inconsistent (), but that calculation does not exclude matrix arguments with different boundary conditions.

Related source comparisons for Problem #257

The following related statements concern Problem #257. They are not inputs to any proof about SS; the comparisons below do not extend the cited statements beyond their hypotheses.

The comparison of the middle-carry estimate () with the remainder estimate () distinguishes the direction of an inequality from control of the required deviation. The associated sign claim in the earlier working notes had no unconditional proof supplied. A sign alone would not give a lower bound for the magnitude in any event.

The row-capacity and later-skip implications retain their respective local deficit and skip hypotheses (, ). The finite-shadow comparison distinguished an existential horizon, obtained from convergence, from the particular horizon J=k−2J=k-2 needed in that application (). The terminal-strip formulation also imposes its own support and carry restrictions (); a bound on carry size does not automatically replace a restriction on the positions of the nonzero coefficients.

For finite sums of 1/(2n−1)1/(2^n-1), the common denominator is odd. Their reduced denominators are therefore odd, so they cannot equal a rational number with even reduced denominator. This is the elementary reason behind the finite-support exclusion and its denominator source (, ). The cited infinite-skipping theorem is stated for the target 1/21/2 (). A proposed extension to other targets requires checking that theorem’s hypotheses and proof; the finite-denominator observation alone does not prove such an extension or the needed infinite-orbit estimate.

Finally, the support-fraction statement and the more general collision bound have distinct hypotheses (, ). The earlier review proposed a broader use but did not supply its additional mean-residue estimate. It also left the endpoint proof bodies in the following dichotomy unverified for a changed target (). No such extension is used here.

Quantifiers must be checked independently.

For example, a statement of the form ∃N∃L∀h\exists N\,\exists L\,\forall h does not provide the required ∀h∀N0∃N≥N0∃L\forall h\,\forall N_0\,\exists N\ge N_0\,\exists L. The first assertion controls many shifts at one location; the second requires arbitrarily late locations for each fixed shift. Relabelling a source statement does not bridge this difference.

Additional mathematics required by the sufficient conditions

The preceding sections contain identities, conditional implications, comparison sequences and finite audits. This section develops the arithmetic estimates needed by the sufficient conditions in Section 3. It separates proved reductions from proposed applications of analytic methods; a limitation of one proposed application is not a theorem excluding the method.

The section contains a doubling-orbit formulation with explicit thresholds, a lacunary comparison sequence for the strength of a block estimate, and sufficient estimates for the prime-factor decomposition. Each result retains its stated evidence label. The discussion of a rank upper bound must also be read with the rational 5/45/4 comparison sequence: rationality alone does not give bounded rank. These are the scope distinctions needed to interpret the individual statements, not priority claims.

Where a claim is proved it is marked [Math]; where it is checked by exact or floating-point computation, [Cert]; where it is quoted, [Cited]; where it is a proposal, [Open]. The proved reductions identify explicit sufficient hypotheses. Those hypotheses remain to be established; the reductions do not prove them.

The phase is a geometrically weighted sum of totients at L+hL+h consecutive arguments. In the first two ranges, 1≤t≤L1\le t\le L, the coefficient has denominator 2t2^t and odd numerator. Its contribution is therefore integral exactly when v2(φ(N+t))≥tv_2(\varphi(N+t))\ge t. In the last range, L<t≤L+hL<t\le L+h, the denominator is instead 2t−h2^{t-h}, so the corresponding threshold is t−ht-h. Here v2(a)v_2(a) denotes the exponent of 22 in the positive integer aa. The selected offset in the four-term decomposition lies in the middle range, where the odd multiplier is 2h−12^h-1.

Relevant comparison estimates.

The following comparisons identify the estimates still needed; they do not rule out these methods.

Weyl differencing and van der Corput. The van der Corput inequality applies to arbitrary bounded complex sequences , but its use here requires estimates for shifted correlations. For the exact phases xN=2Nαhx_N=2^N\alpha_h of Lemma 12.2, xN+q−xN=(2q−1)xN.x_{N+q}-x_N=(2^q-1)x_N. Thus differencing gives another doubling orbit, not a polynomial phase of lower degree. The finite phase D(h,N,L)/2LD(h,N,L)/2^L approximates this orbit modulo 11; it is not the exact orbit itself. No bound for the resulting correlations is established here.

The large sieve. A proposed application would need a suitable family of separated frequencies and a way to recover a bound for each fixed hh. Averaging only over hh would not suffice: the condition asks for a block estimate for every hh, not for most of them.

Bilinear sums over prime factors. Factoring N+t=mpN+t=mp and using φ(mp)=φ(m)(p−1)\varphi(mp)=\varphi(m)(p-1) makes the selected totient contribution linear in the prime pp. Section 12.3 gives this decomposition and identifies the remaining weight. A bound for that weight is still needed before a Vaughan- or Vinogradov-type argument can be applied.

Erdős’s 1948 digit method. The comparison series is E=∑n≥11/(2n−1)=∑N≥1d(N)/2NE=\sum_{n\ge1}1/(2^n-1)=\sum_{N\ge1}d(N)/2^N, whose irrationality Erdős proved [9]. For the totient series, the corresponding Möbius expansion is exact: φ=μ*id\varphi=\mu * \mathrm{id} gives

S=∑d≥1μ(d)2d(2d−1)2\begin{equation} \label{eq:mobmers} S=\sum_{d\ge 1}\mu(d)\,\frac{2^{d}}{(2^{d}-1)^{2}} \end{equation} The identity is labelled [Math]; the recorded numerical check gives S=1.3676308019850223…S=1.3676308019850223\ldots to sixteen digits [Cert].

Erdős combines congruences forcing increasing powers of 22 to divide a block of divisor counts with an averaged tail bound, producing long zero blocks in the binary expansion . To adapt that argument here, one would need congruences for the actual totient coefficients together with a compatible tail estimate. The identities alone provide neither combination. In [eq:mobmers], the coefficients μ(d)\mu(d) can have either sign, so positivity of the original totient series does not give positivity term by term in this expansion. This is a limitation of the proposed direct transfer, not a proof that a digit argument or a different use of the Möbius expansion cannot work.

The unresolved estimate.

For general coefficients 0≤c(n)≤n0\le c(n)\le n, irrationality alone does not imply the block norm condition. The following example has very sparse nonzero coefficients. It is irrational, but almost all phases in each sufficiently large block lie close to 11.

Theorem 12.6 (The block norm condition is stronger in the class 0≤c(n)≤n0\le c(n)\le n). Let c(n)=1c(n)=1 if n=k!n=k! for some k≥1k\ge 1 and c(n)=0c(n)=0 otherwise, so 0≤c(n)≤n0\le c(n)\le n for all n≥1n\ge 1, and let β=∑n≥1c(n)/2n=∑k≥12−k!\beta=\sum_{n\ge1}c(n)/2^{n} =\sum_{k\ge 1}2^{-k!}. Then β\beta is irrational, and for every h≥1h\ge 1 and every X≥81(h+5)X\ge 81(h+5), ∑N=X2X−1cos⁡(2π2N(2h−1)β)>910X.\sum_{N=X}^{2X-1}\cos\bigl(2\pi\,2^{N}(2^{h}-1)\beta\bigr) \;>\; \tfrac{9}{10}X . Consequently the block norm condition fails for β\beta at every sufficiently large scale, for every admissible truncation depth, even though β\beta is irrational. Thus irrationality, nonnegative integer coefficients and the bound c(n)≤nc(n)\le n do not imply the block gap. A proof for SS needs an additional property not shared by this example; the comparison does not specify which additional property will suffice.

The size of the required saving.

Under Lebesgue measure on the phase circle, the binary digit maps are independent fair bits. The digit-change proportion therefore tends to 1/21/2 for almost every phase. For almost every phase, the real-part block sum is also O(Xlog⁡log⁡X)O(\sqrt{X\log\log X}), by the law of the iterated logarithm of Erdős and Gál for lacunary series [27]. The block bound follows by subtracting two initial partial sums. An almost-everywhere theorem supplies no conclusion at the particular phase αh=(2h−1)S\alpha_h=(2^h-1)S [Cited]. The requirement is ρh≥0.11\rho_h\ge 0.11 and a saving of a constant factor. The finite values in Table [tab:blocks] have ρh\rho_h near 0.500.50 and small block averages. They are compatible with square-root cancellation, but do not establish its asymptotic order. The sufficient condition asks only for the stated fixed saving on arbitrarily large blocks. No estimate in this record supplies it for the totient phases.

The remaining prime-weighted correlation.

For N=mp−tN=mp-t, that weight depends on φ(mp+j−t)\varphi(mp+j-t) at the other offsets 1≤j≤L+h1\le j\le L+h, j≠tj\ne t. This fixed-offset example is not Definition 3.4: there ss is fixed while t=L−s+1t=L-s+1 grows. The example isolates a correlation between a quadratic character at pp and the binary phases of totients at p+1,p+2,…p+1,p+2,\ldots. It is analogous in this respect to shifted correlations studied in the Chowla and Elliott problems, but the analogy does not supply an applicable theorem. The cited theorems have different hypotheses and types of average: Matomäki and Radziwiłł compare short and long averages of real multiplicative functions bounded by 11, outside an exceptional set of short intervals [22]; Tao proves logarithmically averaged two-point Chowla and a corrected Elliott statement, the latter under an explicit non-pretentiousness hypothesis on one of the bounded multiplicative functions  [23]; and Tao and Teräväinen prove the odd-order logarithmically averaged Chowla conjecture  [Cited]. The phase here depends on φ\varphi at a growing window of shifts, so none of these applies directly.

Averaging over the block parameter.

For each fixed hh, an average of the nonnegative, normalised block norms can establish the full-block condition. It is enough to prove ∑k=1K2−k|∑N=2k2k+1−1e(D(h,N,Lk)/2Lk)|=o(K),\sum_{k=1}^{K}2^{-k} \left|\sum_{N=2^k}^{2^{k+1}-1} e\bigl(D(h,N,L_k)/2^{L_k}\bigr)\right|=o(K), where every LkL_k satisfies the room inequality for X=2kX=2^k. Indeed, the number of k≤Kk\le K for which the normalised norm exceeds 21/2521/25 is at most 25/2125/21 times the displayed sum, hence is o(K)o(K). There are therefore arbitrarily large admissible blocks satisfying Definition 3.1. This argument does not establish the four-term condition: that condition requires all four separate budgets with common X,L,s,ηX,L,s,\eta.

The displayed average is a Cesàro average of norms on dyadic blocks. It is not the signed logarithmically weighted correlation appearing in the cited Chowla–Elliott theorems. The position of the absolute value matters: cancellation between different blocks would not bound this sum of norms. Invoking entropy decrement would therefore require an additional argument yielding this particular estimate.

The finite phase depends on the L+hL+h totient values at offsets 1,…,L+h1,\ldots,L+h, with the coefficients in [eq:window]. Although its absolute value is 11, it is not a multiplicative function of NN. Both the number of shifts and their dyadic denominators grow with LL. The cited fixed-shift correlation theorems do not supply the uniform bounds for this growing family. No such extension is proved here. [Open]

What the prime condition adds.

The preceding condition asks for a separated point at a prime-indexed position. The full-block average does not by itself locate such a point on a prescribed sparse set. Conversely, the prime condition does not assert cancellation over the whole interval. They are different sufficient hypotheses; no general comparison of their difficulty is proved here.

Comparison with digit complexity.

The phase inequality above is a quantitative statement at specified positions and period multiples. A general block-complexity assertion is a different quantified statement, of the kind treated by the Adamczewski–Bugeaud method for algebraic numbers [25]. No implication from such an assertion to the required inequality is established here. In particular, this record does not justify describing one existing method as the only possible route, or algebraicity as the sole missing input. The arithmetic nonintegrality obligation must be stated and proved in its own right.

The rank quantities.

Finite-dimensional span of all dyadic sections is the definition of a 22-regular sequence in the sense of Allouche and Shallit [1] [Cited]. For integer-valued sequences this is equivalent to finite generation of the ℤ\mathbb Z-module generated by the sections: if their span has dimension dd, some dd evaluations embed it in ℚd\mathbb Q^d and that module in ℤd\mathbb Z^d [Math]. Coons  proved that φ\varphi is not kk-regular for any k≥2k\ge2 [Cited]. The unconditional theorem proves the case k=2k=2 independently. For integer coefficient and carry sequences, the recurrence transfers non-22-regularity of the coefficients to non-22-regularity of the carry. A proof must include the zero-residue sections, not just the positive residues. The following argument gives an explicit dimension bound.

For a rational-valued sequence ff, let Ve(f)V_e(f) be the span of all its sections through levels 0,…,e0,\ldots,e. Define the backward shift by (Bf)(0)=0(Bf)(0)=0 and (Bf)(n)=f(n−1)(Bf)(n)=f(n-1) for n≥1n\ge1, and let δ0\delta_0 be 11 at 00 and 00 elsewhere. A level-jj section of BfBf is a section of ff if its residue is positive. At residue zero it is the backward shift of n↦f(2jn+2j−1)n\mapsto f(2^jn+2^j-1). Hence Ve(Bf)⊆Ve(f)+B(Ve(f)).V_e(Bf)\subseteq V_e(f)+B(V_e(f)). For integer sequences c,uc,u and a positive integer vv, the recurrence vc(n+1)=2u(n)−u(n+1)v c(n+1)=2u(n)-u(n+1) gives c=2Bu−uv+(c(0)+u(0)v)δ0.c=\frac{2Bu-u}{v}+\left(c(0)+\frac{u(0)}v\right)\delta_0. Since every section of δ0\delta_0 is 00 or δ0\delta_0, it follows that Ve(c)⊆Ve(u)+B(Ve(u))+ℚδ0,dim⁡ℚVe(c)≤2dim⁡ℚVe(u)+1.V_e(c)\subseteq V_e(u)+B(V_e(u))+\mathbb{Q}\delta_0, \qquad \dim_{\mathbb{Q}} V_e(c)\le2\dim_{\mathbb{Q}} V_e(u)+1. In particular, bounded carry ranks would force bounded coefficient ranks. Non-22-regularity of cc therefore forces unbounded carry ranks. This is an ordinary proof, not a claim of a new Lean declaration. It also gives the generic bound dim⁡ℚVe(u)≥2e−1\dim_{\mathbb{Q}} V_e(u)\ge2^{e-1} for c=φc=\varphi and e≥1e\ge1, using the coefficient rank 2e+12^e+1. The factor 22 is not an additive O(1)O(1) loss, and this bound concerns all sections, including level zero. [Math]

The source theorem for φ\varphi is sharper: the carry sections at all residues of levels 1,…,e1,\ldots,e have rank at least 2e−12^e-1. It uses the independence of the odd-residue totient sections. Neither lower bound is an irrationality proof, since rational coefficient series can have nonregular carries. The separate 5/45/4 comparison verifies this directly. Any proposed rank upper bound must use additional totient-specific hypotheses not satisfied by the 5/45/4 comparison sequence.

The first four conditions concern the same constant but impose different averaging, sampling and separation requirements. The 11/10011/100 digit-change test in Corollary 12.4 is sufficient for a real-part bound; it is not a replacement for the norm or four-term rows. Only the full-depth row is proved here to be equivalent to irrationality. The last row records a false generic upper bound, not an additional open hypothesis.

Quantitative estimates.

The counterexamples identify missing assumptions in the specific arguments tested here. They do not imply that the binary digits of SS are random, normal, or unusually structured. A constructed counterexample can disprove an implication without resembling SS in other respects. Likewise, failure of one congruence construction does not exclude every use of the Chinese remainder theorem.

Additional arithmetic information.

Table [tab:blocks] records finite observations: the sampled digit-change proportions are near 0.500.50, above the sufficient threshold 0.110.11, and the displayed normalized cosine sums are below 0.890.89. These computations are compatible with the proposed conditions. They do not establish those conditions for every shift and arbitrarily large blocks, or prove a fair-coin model for the digits. The relevant quantified estimates remain unproved here.

The recorded small margins near a forbidden endpoint also require careful interpretation. One small margin disproves a proposed lower bound larger than that margin at that index. It does not rule out every positive margin on a suitable subsequence, or every estimate with scale-dependent bounds. No numerical census in this record determines which of these possibilities holds asymptotically.

Scope of the comparison.

Corollary 12.4 specifies one sufficient digit statistic: for every fixed hh, the digit-change proportion must reach at least 11/10011/100 on arbitrarily large blocks. A statement for one shift, a smaller positive proportion, or finitely many blocks is not this hypothesis. An upper bound o(N)o(N) on the longest run alone would not imply irrationality; a periodic alternating expansion has bounded runs. The prime-index condition in [eq:primefibre] is another proposed sufficient estimate. Its exact algebraic decomposition does not establish the required correlation bound.

Certificate completeness

The block exponential-sum condition

A bound for an exponential sum is sufficient for the quantified residue condition. With e(x)=exp⁡(2πix)e(x)=\exp(2\pi i x), the assertion is block norm condition:≡∀h>0,∀X0,∃X,L,max⁡(X0,1)≤X∧16(2X+h+L+2)≤2L∧∥∑N∈[X,2X)e(D(h,N,L)/2L)∥≤2125X.\text{block norm condition} :\equiv\ \forall h>0,\ \forall X_0,\ \exists X,L,\quad \max(X_0,1)\le X\ \wedge\ 16\,(2X+h+L+2)\le 2^L\ \wedge\ \Bigl\|\sum_{N\in[X,2X)} e\bigl(D(h,N,L)/2^L\bigr)\Bigr\| \le \tfrac{21}{25}X.

(the universally quantified assertion is not proved) .

block norm condition⇒S∉ℚ.\text{block norm condition} \ \Longrightarrow\ S\notin\mathbb Q. . The

threshold is X0X_0, while XX and LL are chosen witnesses and may depend on both hh and X0X_0. Taking X0=N0X_0=N_0 gives a certificate at some N∈[X,2X)N\in[X,2X), hence at N≥N0N\ge N_0. The elementary reason is that, if every residue failed the test, each would be within (2X+h+L+2)/2L≤1/16(2X+h+L+2)/2^L\le1/16 of an integer. Every summand would then have real part at least cos⁡(π/8)>21/25\cos(\pi/8)>21/25, contradicting the norm bound. The implication is proved; the bound on suitable blocks beyond every threshold remains to be established.

The underlying finite lemma is more general: it applies to any nonempty finite T⊆[0,2X)T\subseteq[0,2X) with the stated size bound and ∥∑N∈Te(D(h,N,L)/2L)∥≤(21/25)|T|\|\sum_{N\in T}e(D(h,N,L)/2^L)\|\le(21/25)|T|. Taking T=[X,2X)T=[X,2X) gives the full-block implication. Allowing a chosen subset weakens the hypothesis; it does not strengthen it. The source uses the elementary block lemma ([Lean], unconditional as an implication). The real-part version uses Re⁡∑N∈Te(D(h,N,L)/2L)≤(9/10)|T|\operatorname{Re}\sum_{N\in T}e(D(h,N,L)/2^L)\le(9/10)|T|. Its proof uses cos⁡(π/8)>9/10\cos(\pi/8)>9/10 and averaging. An unspecified saving below |T||T| is not the stated hypothesis.

What supplying this form would take: genuine cancellation for the additive character e(D(h,N,L)/2L)e(D(h,N,L)/2^L) at the growing dyadic moduli permitted by the size bound. The quantifiers require suitable blocks beyond every threshold for each fixed h>0h>0; they do not require one threshold that works simultaneously for all hh. gives a comparison in which every weighted phase equals 11 while the specified determinant remains nonzero. Thus nonvanishing of that determinant alone cannot prove cancellation. A successful use of a determinant would need further information connecting its entries to the phase sum; the comparison does not exclude every such argument.

Farey growth and the failed generic rank argument

The Farey growth law below is a separate unproved assertion. The rank statement is retained only to record a counterfactual sufficient input and the reason that the generic compression route to it is closed; it is not a second open problem supported by the present argument.

The hypothetical rank bound.

Unconditionally, for every level e≥1e\ge1, the dyadic totient basis of 2e+12^e+1 sequences is linearly independent over ℚ\mathbb{Q} (via CRT and Dirichlet’s theorem on primes in arithmetic progression): . Consequently, if S∈ℚS\in\mathbb{Q}, there is an integer v>0v>0 with vS∈ℤvS\in\mathbb{Z}. It obeys uN+1=2uN−vφ(N+1)u_{N+1}=2u_N-v\varphi(N+1) and 0≤uN≤v(N+2)0\le u_N\le v(N+2). .

A bound independent of ee for these same carry-section ranks would contradict the displayed lower bound; so would an upper bound that is o(2e)o(2^e). Growth of the Farey denominator bound.

The finite denominator exclusion for SS comes from a Farey-gap denominator exclusion at a single fixed window K=240K=240: S≠a/bfor all a∈ℤ,1≤b≤79639646646701375323355774875831053,gcd⁡(a,b)=1.S\ne a/b\quad\text{for all }a\in\mathbb{Z},\quad 1\le b\le79639646646701375323355774875831053, \quad\gcd(a,b)=1. . This bound is sharp at K=240K=240; the mediant denominator q=79639646646701375323355774875831054q=79639646646701375323355774875831054 is the exact first failing denominator (, [Lean]); so the same interval cannot exclude every rational at the next denominator. A different window requires a new certificate or a uniform argument; the fixed-window calculation supplies neither.

A sufficient extension is a function g(K)→∞g(K)\to\infty for which every (N=1,K)(N=1,K) gap check excludes all rationals of reduced denominator at most g(K)g(K). More generally, unbounded valid exclusion bounds along a sequence of windows suffice. This is a statement about the certified intervals. The record does not prove it equivalent to a lower bound on the continued-fraction denominators of SS. [Open] [cofinal] .

For pp prime and e≥1e\ge1, a successful unit-gap certificate at denominator pep^e has zero candidates or a single candidate divisible by pp; . The success hypothesis is essential: the bound is not a statement about every window at that denominator. Nor does it bound the eventual denominator cutoff. The prime-power restriction cannot be omitted, as the modulo-1515 example in Observation 6.114 shows. No obstruction to a uniform estimate as KK varies is proved here.

Reading the table. “Sufficient” records only the indicated implication. It does not assert a converse or a strict comparison of strength. “Equivalent” records two proved directions, either directly or through the base equivalence with S∉ℚS\notin\mathbb Q. Logical equivalence does not by itself provide a direct construction from the finite witnesses in one formulation to those in another.

What remains to be proved

The implications above leave explicit arithmetic assertions to prove for φ\varphi. Two types of estimate can be stated directly, without assuming either that they follow from known methods or that they exhaust the possible approaches.

Exponential sums.

For each fixed h>0h>0 and every threshold X0X_0, the block norm condition asks for some X≥max⁡(X0,1)X\ge\max(X_0,1) and LL satisfying both the modulus bound and |∑N∈[X,2X)e(D(h,N,L)/2L)|≤2125X.\left|\sum_{N\in[X,2X)}e\bigl(D(h,N,L)/2^L\bigr)\right| \le\frac{21}{25}X. The saving 21/2521/25 is fixed, but the chosen block and depth may depend on hh and X0X_0; uniformity of these choices in hh is not required. The preceding four-term decomposition and the proved counting bounds identify contributions to this sum. The two remaining weighted estimates must still be obtained with the same parameters. The record therefore gives an exact reduction and some of its estimates, not a proof of the displayed cancellation bound.

The last totient difference.

The endpoint criteria compare δ2a(2q+2)=φ(2H+2q+2)−φ(H+2q+2),H=H2a,\delta_{2^a}(2q+2) =\varphi(2H+2q+2)-\varphi(H+2q+2),\qquad H=H_{2^a}, with twice the centred residue ua,qu_{a,q}. An appropriate inequality, proved for arbitrarily large aa with the stated bounds on qq, would contradict the carry interval required by integrality. The exact identity explains why such an inequality would suffice; it does not supply the inequality. The finite examples through t=82t=82, and the short-window examples at a=4,6a=4,6, do not establish an asymptotic pattern.

Declarations

Further background.

Erick Wong posted a proof that ∑n≥1(φ(n)mod⁡k)k−n\sum_{n\ge1}(\varphi(n)\operatorname{mod} k)k^{-n} is irrational for every integer k>2k>2 on Mathematics Stack Exchange on 29 March 2015 [5]; there the base equals the modulus. The Möbius-square form of SS and its coprimality interpretation were posted publicly before this record, as credited in §5.4. Kovač and Tao show that suitable subsums of Lambert series in distinct integer bases can be rational ; the freedom to choose those subsums is absent for SS. The Lambert-series factorisations of Merca [15] and of Merca and Schmidt  are transform background for the Möbius–Mersenne coordinate. Balasubramanian, Giri and Srivastav prove asymptotics for finite shifted convolutions of divisor-convolution functions, including φ(n)/n\varphi(n)/n, uniformly for |h|≤x/2|h|\le x/2 at cutoff xx . Their partial-summation extension uses differentiable weights with bounded derivative on the summation interval [17]. Applying that observation here would require control of the weighted error for the present phases; no such estimate is established in this record. The cited results are not themselves the dyadic residue separation required by Sep\mathrm{Sep}. The remaining sources are cited where their hypotheses are used.

At the generating-function level, the published height criterion of Adamczewski, Bell and Smertnig gives kk-regularity for a kk-Mahler series with integer coefficients of polynomial growth  . For the totient coefficients the logarithmic heights are log⁡max⁡(1,φ(n))≤log⁡n\log\max(1,\varphi(n))\le\log n for n≥1n\ge1, so Coons’s nonregularity already rules out kk-Mahler equations in every base. The later multiplicative classification of Bell and Smertnig provides another route [30]. The algebraic and DD-finite classifications of Bell, Bruin and Coons belong to the same function-level context [31]. They do not by themselves decide the value at z=1/2z=1/2.

Automatic prime-sampling theorems address a different issue. Adamczewski, Drmota and Müllner identify a computable local coprimality condition governing the relevant logarithmic densities, with a conditional ordinary-density transfer [32]. Their theorem does not assert that every output state has positive density on a prescribed prime progression, nor does it prove independence with automatic coefficient weights. Any use for that purpose needs its own compatibility argument. [Cited]

Sources and data.

The linked Lean declarations, fixed toolchain, and library manifest are published in the companion repository. The ordinary arguments in these papers explain the mathematics; the pinned declarations record the corresponding formal statements. Their hypotheses must be checked separately when an implication is applied.

Formalisation coverage and remaining dependencies

Every theorem, lemma, proposition and corollary of this record other than the five listed below has a Lean statement of the same assertion, with the same hypotheses, checked by the Lean kernel using only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, in the development at revision 181078b6b009.

Proposition 12.7, one of the five, was proved later. It has a Lean statement of the same assertion, checked by the Lean kernel using only those three axioms, at revision e4ba6841dfdb; the paragraph after its proof describes the Lean argument.

Propositions 5.17 and 6.30 share one input. The displayed three-term identity is unconditional and checked in both. The development verifies the reduction of the irrationality clause to the theorem of Postelmans and Van Assche that 11, ζq(1)\zeta_q(1) and ζq(2)\zeta_q(2) are linearly independent over ℚ\mathbb{Q} for q=1/pq=1/p with an integer p≥2p\ge2 . A formal proof of that input is not included in the verified development, so those two endpoints remain conditional on it. Proposition 6.102 is the same situation with a different input. Its four Lambert identities and the identification of L(Id)L(\mathrm{Id}) with ∑m≥1σ(m)/2m\sum_{m\ge1}\sigma(m)/2^m are checked, and the development verifies the reduction of the transcendence of that value to Nesterenko’s theorem on the algebraic independence of the three Eisenstein values at an algebraic point of the punctured unit disc [11].

Proposition 12.8 is checked in Lean with the prime number theorem as its one input (prop_badcof, revision 76f44c5329c0). Its density D(η)D(\eta) enters as the premise that B(η)B(\eta) has a natural density, which the statement takes from Schoenberg’s theorem.

A theorem whose own statement is conditional is formalised exactly as stated. Propositions 5.17, 6.30, 6.102 and 12.8 are asserted unconditionally in this record, and all four have Lean counterparts carrying a named input.

Concordance of statements and Lean declarations.

Each result of this record that has a kernel-checked Lean statement of the same assertion is listed below with the declarations that jointly state it. Each name links to its declaration at revision a25cb360bef8. Where the Lean statement is stronger than the printed one and implies it by an immediate specialisation, the entry says so. An entry marked compared was also checked independently: a restatement of the same declarations against Mathlib alone, together with its proof, was verified by Comparator (leanprover/comparator) in a clean continuous integration environment, in the run named by its number. Comparator trusts the restated statement, so the correspondence between the printed result and that statement is the one this concordance records.

Verification scope.

Kernel checking validates a formal proof of its stated proposition relative to the declared axioms. It does not check that every prose summary has the same hypotheses or verify the literature comparisons. In particular, a checked implication with an unproved hypothesis is not a proof that Problem 249 is solved.
